Si, this Bth January, 1885, the following Bill was considered, namely : A Bill intituled A Bill to authorise the Construction of a Ship Canal to Manchester, aid for other purposes." 4nd the following resolutions were passed, namely That the Board do oppose the same, and that the Clerk and Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., solicitors, be and they are hereby empowered and instructed to take all necessary steps by Petition to Parliament and otherwise for giving effect to such opposition, and for the protection of the rights and in- terests of tha Bard and of the District of Widnes in relation to the objects of such Bill." PASTEUR'S WORD TO YOUNG MEN. 7ai toujours aime la jeunesse. Du plus, loin gull me souvienne dans ma vie d'homme, je ne erois pas avoir jamais aborde un -fitudiant sans lui dire; travaille et persZvere. •Le travail amuse et seal ii profite h l'homme, an citoyen, a la patrie. Brace up your wills, brave-hearted boys, To mingle hardship with your joys, In life's abundant measure; Put hand to plough, and persevere, gink When skies are dark, when skies are clear, For labour is the title here That gives a claim to pleasure. Who's he that feeds his soul with fears, IC. And makes sweet luxury of tears, And cradles dainty sorrow; At every breath of harm who frets, a._„. And grumbles when his shoes he wets, And on a rainy day forgets That suns will shine to-morrow. Where would he live? In some soft spot • Where all things can for all be got Without or toil or trouble! rE• What sport were this, with nothing hard To do, no hindrance to retard, _ No risk to run, and one reward For all—a floating bubble! Leave dreams to Fools! The name of Life • Is work—a various-mingled strife Of Powers that slumber never; o._ The swelling seas, the circling spheres, The racing winds, the rolling years, V The fateful tide of hopes and fears, • z- Work bravely on for ever! Work—not alone,—we work with God, His tools to stir the teeming sod, Or load the fruitful river`; And if it chance His work we mar, - With limping faith, or loveless war, ' His touch to music turns the jar, " With strength that faileth never. Trench deep the soil; cast bi oad the seeds, And branchingArees o'er noxious weeds Will spread their fruitful measure. Put hand to plough, and persevere, When skies are dark, when skies are clear; For labour is the relish here • That gives a zest to pleasure !, "S4nday Talk." JOHN 8117 ART BLASIE.

14 FATHER'S COMING." Oh, Father is coming! - Through all the long day We thought of him often, When he was away; We knew he was working While we were at play. He'll be tired, I think; I have set him a chair In his own cosy corner— He likes to sit there— ' And we'll bring him his slippers, His old favourite pair. I think it's the nicest ; To watch at the gate; And Dolly sits by us While thus we all wait. He'll be here very soon— It's so seldom he's late,
• See, Baby knows too Who is coming to-night; She is crowing, and clapping • Her hands with delight! There's his footstep at last! Oh, hurrah! he's in sight. Folks' Magazine

A play is said to "run" when it stays a long time at one theatre. A wall in the southern part of China is said to be ma-le entirely of fish. It ought to be an easy one to Scale. Old Henry VIII. was an eccentric wooer. He never popped the question. He just married a woman, and then axed her afterwards. An Irish °facer, giving orders to a sentinel, com- manded him "not to stir a foot, but walk up and down, tend see what he could bear." A man whose knowledge is based on actual experience says that when callhig on their sweethearts, young men should carry affection in their hearts, perfection in their manners, and confection in their pockets. Not long ago a Scottish clergyman reproved a member of his flock for being drunk. " Gin it please ye;' said 3emn,iy, "I dinna drink as meilde as yersel.' "Why, how is that?" said the minister. "Aweel, dinna ye talc a glass o' whusky and water after dinner?" "Why, yes, Jemmy, sure I take a glass of whisky after dinner, to aid digestion." "And dinna ye tak a glass o' toddy every nicht when ye are ganging to bed ?" "Yes, to be sure, I just take a little toddy every night to help me to - •• • • -

• _ sleep." "Well," continued Jemmy, "that's just four- -, teen glasses a week, and about sixty every month. I • only get paid once a month, and then if Pd. tak sixty glasses it wud mak me dead drunk for a week.. Now, ye see, the only difference is that ye time it better than 1 do." Mogan:wry IN larzmios.—Morbidity in religion might be partially cured by more out-door exercise. There are some duties we can perform better on our feet than on our knees. If we can carry the grace of God with us down intp every day practical Christian work, we will , get more spiritual strength in five minutes than by ten hours of kneeling. If Daniel had not served God save when three times a day he worshipped toward the temple, the lions would have surely eaten him up. The school of Christ is as much out-doors as in-doors. Hard, rough work for God will Oevelop an athletic souL Re- lig,ion will not conquer either -the admiration or the affections of men by effeminacy but by strength. Be- cause the heart is soft is no reason why the head should be soft. The spirit of genuine'religion is a spirit Of great power. When Christ rides in apocalyptic vision it IS not on a weak and stupid beast, but on a horse emblem of majesty and strength : "And he went forth conquering and to conquer."----lar. Talmage. The patriots of New England, who laboured to secure self-government for the colonies, had to encounter their neighbours, who were devoted to the King and Parlia- ment. Among these loyalists was found here and there a clergyman who thought it his duty to preach the sub- mission of subjects and the right of rulers. One of these clergymen was the Rev. Mr. Chase, of Portsmouth, N. H., who numbered among his congregation Captain John Blunt, shipmaster and farmer. On the birth of the captain's sixth boy, it was determined, after a family censultation, to name him William, and he was carried to the church to be christened. It happened on that Sunday morning that the Rev. Mr. Chase, bent on eradicating the growing disloyalty of his people, preached a sermon in denunciation of Oliver Cromwell as a blas- phemous revolutionist. Captain Blunt, being an out- spoken patriot, determined to resent the minister's attack on the Puritan hero. "What is his name ?" asked the clergyman, as the child was placed in hi arms. "Oliver Cromwell,: replied the captain, in a distinct tone. " What—what did you say, sir ?" asked the amazed foinister, gasping as if he had been struck. "Oliver Cromwell, sir," said the captain, in a voice as stentorian &3 if shouted to his men in a gale. And the boy was christettod Oliver Cromwell Blunt. WHAT is Mita ?—" All language has a tendency to deteriorate, but that is no reason why respectableawords like ' milk' should ha.-e a push down hill given them by persons in authority. This is what has happened in the eaae of 'Lane v. Collins,' noted in last week's Notes of Gases. The Adulteration Act, 1875, requires, under penalties, that articles of food sold shall be of the nature, substance, and quality' of the article demanded, and Mr. Justice Day and Mr. Justice Mathew decide that when 'milk' is asked for the statute is sufficiently complied with if skimmed milk is supplied, that is to say, 80 per cent. deficient in butter-fat. Skimmed milk, they lay down, is the milk of commerce, but the ques- tion is whether it is-the milk of language. We venture to maintain that milk' means the milk of the cow, and that those who want cow's milk do not use a negative and ask for unskimmed milk.' The impetus:now given to the decline of language in the interests of commerce may carry us far. If we ask for coal,' we are not en- titled to co d as it comes from the pit, butymust be satisfied with dregs, from which, in the words of:the play, all the knobbly ones' have been picked out. If we ask for strawberries, we must put up with a basket of leavings with a few big fruit at the top. If we ask for wine, we must, on the authority of these learned Judges, be content to drink, horresctmus„ the claret of commerce."—Law Journa/. THAT BUGBEAR COLD.—CoId as a bugbear plays much- mischief in the nursery. Thousands of; children in this country are coddled to death and many actually stifled in bed. They call it being overlaid; it is being smothered. That is the right name for it. But children must be kept warm? Bless their innocence! yes. The bed as soft as down, the clothes as soft as soft can be, but smooth withal, without any tendency to rumple up, or cover mouqx or face. This is warmth; this is com- fort. The room, too, should be moderately warm; no more, I pray you; and the air ought to be as pure and Sweet as the odour of roses. Is it so in most nurseries? Nay, for your bugbear cold steps in and seals doors and . windows. No wonder that when baby wakes up it is peevish and fretful. Your bugbear cold is the best friend the tailor has, for even young men wear double the weight of clothes'on a winter's day that they ought to. They sweat themselves in consequence,ao cold the foe steps in and ends many a life. Topcoats, in my opinion should never be worn except while riding by rail, or driving, or when standing about in a draught; then they cannot be too thick and cosy. If worn at all when walking they should be very thin. Very light waterproofs should be worn while walking in winter— worn over the arm, I mean, and never put on the back, except when it is raining. But the warmer the socks the better, and the shoes ought to be moderately strong and thick, for many an ailment is caught from standing .*out on cold damp ground. At their conclusion the learned Judge stated that he should write to the Secretary of State at Washington recommending his extradition. The Government autho- rities, however, have now decided not to give up Rae- side, the ground of their refusal being that the offence with which he is charged is not covered by the treaty. It appears that one of the provisions of the treaty is that no person shall be extradited for an offence that is not a crime in the country in which he has taken refuge. /3y the statute law of Illinois, forgery is not a crime re- cognised by statute law unless it can be shown that the persons whose names are forged have suffered damage, or could be rendered liable to a legal claim. There are several states in the Union in which the law is not thu hedged in. EUROPEAN DUTIES ON CORN.—As the French Govern- ment has now made known the amount of duty which it will consent to lay on foreign corn, it is of general interest to establish by a comparison with other coun- tries the position France will -be in if the Chamberh adopt and ratify the proposals of the Cabinet. Those proposals are that a duty of 2f. 60c. shall be levied on ever/13.00 kilogrammes of corn imported into France, and that he tax on the same quantity of flour shall be sf. 20c. There are six European countries—England, Bel- , gium, Denmark, Sweden, the Netherlands, and Russia— in which corn does aot pay any import duty at all. In the tither European States the import duty on corn and dour, expressed in francs and centimes, and per 100 kilo- graniunes is—Switzerland, corn, 30c., flour if.; Norway, corn 28c., flour if. 710.; Italy, corn if. 40c., flour 2f. 77c.; Germany, corn if. 25c., flour, 3f. 75c. ; Austria-Hungary, corn,lf. 25c., flour 3f. 75c.; Greece, corn if. 41c., flour 3f. 51c.; Spain, corn 4f. 20c., flour Of.; Portugal, corn sf. 60c., flour Bf. 96c.; Turkey, corn Bf. Ioc., flour 8 per cent. It therefore follows that if, instead of maintaining the existing import duty of 60e. on corn and if. 2c. on flour, the Chambers vote the Government proposals, and raise it to 2f. 60c. on corn and sf. 20c. on flour, bread will not only be dearer in France than in England, Belgium, Den- mark, Sweden, the Netherlands, and Russia—where, no import duty is levied on corn,—but also dearer than in Switzerland, Norwtiy, Italy, Germany, Austria, and Greece, where the duty would be lower.

div.p: ---- - THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.

THE COCHIN. Some of the readers of this journal are in the "Fifties" will probably remember the days when the Cochin China fowl created such a sensation in this country. About 35 years ago this breed of fowls was the mania of the day. It was vaunted to the skies as the best, the most prolific, the handsomest bird that was ever seen. To possess a pair of these fowls meant for- tune, so it was said. The hens would lay several eggs a day, of the richest colour and flavour, and fabulous prices, even compared with prices now realised for first- class exhibition birds, were realised for specimens. Fifty pounds for a cock or five bounds for a setting of eggs was no uncommon price. Poultry shows were then the resort of fashionable folk, and crowds thronged them, struggling almost for the right to be there. But it was not long ere the bubble burst, and the much-vaunted merits of ;the fowl found to exist only in the imagina- tion of those who puffed up the breed. The whim of fashionable society passed away, poultry shows became comparatively deserted, the mania died out. The Cochin China fowl was first known under the name of Shanghaes, a title given to all birds from the Celestial Empire. The first recorded importation took place in 1845, though about two or three years before that specimens of the breed had been seen by officers of both the army and navy in China. In the year named her Majesty the Queen received several birds of this breed, and exhibited them at the Show of the Royal Dublin Society in the April of 1848. At a show held at the Zoological Gardens, London, in 1845, prizes were specially given to Malays and other Asiatic breeds, but none of the Shanghaes or Cochins were exhibited, which would not have been the case had any been in the 'noun- try. In works on Poultry published in 1842, now in possession of the writer, there is no mention of this breed, nor in another work issued in 1847 is there any description of them, showing that at these times they were unknown. But as already stated, when once im- ported they very rapidly advanced in popular favour. The example of the Queen would have much to do with this, and the novel appearance of the fowls,. with their I feathered legs, buff or partridge plumage, quiet de- meanour; and scimitar-shaped tail feathers*, made it en- tirely. distinct from any race of domestic poultry then known irr this country. Reproduction soon extended the numbers of the fowls, but yet not equal to the de- Mend, and those who were fortunate enough to possess imported birds really made littlefertunes by the sale of eggs and chickens. Asia always- the case, much exag- geration took .place. The large size was greatly magni- fied, and the hoarse crow was even said to be nearly as loud as the roar of a lion. We all know how this sort of thing goes on and it accounts for that maniarwhich theugh it passed away, left ar permanent interest in poultry that has steadily increased to the present day. Strange it is that this mania should have been respect- ing:a breed which had and has so little to recommend it, from an economio point of view, It cannot' be said to be algood layer. The eggs, it is true, are very rich in flavour, with a high colour which always makes them popular, but they are small compared with the size of the hen, running about nine to the pound. Cochins are most indefatigable .sitters. As soon as they-have pro- duced a dozen eggs they want to sit, and whilst this quality is very useful at times,, it is very annoying, at other: seasons. Cochins have certainly the merit of lay- ing well in winter, due probably to their profuse feather- ing, which prevents undue evaporation of heat. Young ohickens are tender and fairly good on the table, but when older they cannot be regarded as oven passable in. that respect The flesh is at times very yellow, and more largely developed on the- thighs than thesbreast. This is due to the fact that Cochins are not flyers. They have-only small wings, whilst very large ones would be needed to support such a heavy frame. As it is one of Nature's rules never to develop that which is not re- quired, the muscles of the breast are small, whilst those of the thighs and legs are large. The weighe which Cochins attain is very good indeed. Adult cocks, r4nge from twelve to fifteen pounds; hens eight to, eleven pounds; and cockerels and pullets two or three-pounds less- They are very hardy, mad stand almost' any place and,soil, but do best on short level grass, or the foot feather is broken and spoiled. We know some-breeders of exhibition Cochins who pay as much attention to the grass in their runs as can be given to any lawn. And it undoubtedly pays them to do so. The chickens are easy to rear, but are slow in earning to full growth. They hare another failing also, namely, that cocks cannot be relied upon as breeders after they are three-years old. And at that age the hens are very poor layers, There are four colours:of Cochins at present known, namely—Buff or Cinnamon (which are simply. two 'shades of one colour), Partridge, Whites, and Blacks. :The two first named, the Buffs and the Fartridge, are the ;Most popular, the former especially being largely exhi- '.bited, and at such shows as Birmingham, the. numbers ;and quality are really wonderful. They are, from a purely exhibition point of view, the most symmetrical and perfect of all breeds of domestic poultry, arid from the economic side they are perhaps the worst of all the heavier breeds, and consequently whilst giving these full details respecting them, we.cannot recommend them to farmers and ordinary poultry keepers, except good sit- ters and mothers. are required. Of the four varieties, the Partridge and the Blacks are,, we think, the best layers. In this district there are many- good breeders of Cochins, the Buffs and Partridge-especially—Mrs. Barton, (of Carnfortkr, Mr. Stretch (of Ormakirk), Mr. Bigg (of Ulverston), and Mr. Hind (of Kendal) being noted win- ners with the former; and Ein J. Wood (of Brinseall, Chorley), le, R. Southern (of Woraley), and Mr. Shexpe of KendaD with the latter.

FENIAN OUTRAGE IN NEW YORK A desperate and premeditated attempt to assassinate sn Irish-American was made in New York on Friday afternoon at O'Donovanßossa's office. One Captain Phelan, who was the superintendent of the workhouse in Kansas City, rEceivrd some time ago a written request to call at O'Donovan Rossa's office. He accordingly did so, and met there Ro- bert Short, whose name Phelan afterwards stated is Barker. Barker rushed upon Phelan with a large double-edged dirk, and after inflicting six deadly wounds with this wef,pon fired at his victim with a revolver. Phelan was a mambo of the dynamite party, and was concerned in the attempt Is destroy the steamship Queen. He was stabbed eleven times. times, but did not die as was at fist reported. A later account says that Captain Phelan was taken un- awares, but he immediately armed himself with a revolver, and fired at his assailant, seriously wounding him. Captain Phelan is one of the projectors of the skirmishing fund started by the extreme Irishmen in New York ti collect money for the purposes of dynamite outrages ia Englan_„d* Re *as once suspected of having been the celebratod an" I much talked of No. I. Short declared that Phelan was °Be of the many Irishmen who had been driven to take refuge in America on account of the revelations made by M‘Dermott, the informer, to the English Government. 1.13.:/_ cause of Short's action is said to be that Phelan bad rh- valged certain secrets of the Fenian Society. A letter fres°. Rossa was found on Phelan's person inviting him ro :hie office to discuss important business. There is., alc, mense excitement in the Irish Fenian colony in New who surrounded the office of United It eland in Chamber°. street, threatening death to O'Donovan Roan, who was, however, protected by his friends. • The final issue of this tragedy, and perhaps the only 532. 'Mastery one, is that the entire set of Irish conspirators 11 New York are now in peril of imprisonment. The'l York press, which has consistently held Rosa to be the ; head of a few boasting braggarts, living under the shelter of the American flag, on the proceeds of newspaper blosln, , aboat dynamite outrages, now takes the view that they after all, be" skulking assassins," and, if so, must be flea with promptly and with unsparing severity. On Monday, Richard Short, alias Barker, who was arrrettrl ted directly after Phelan had shot him, was charged stabbing Phelan, and remanded. It is thought l'he'% will recover. Phelan, it is said, was staying with friends lu Cork at the time of the Liverpool dynamite trials in Whi4_,. he took great interest. As a "suspect " he had been.e.e;. amined by the Irish police, and his luggage searched. Ftn,."a ing nothing incriminating, the police released him, and took an early chance to quietly return to America. Phec is reputed to have believed McDermott to be an 1,,,. former. Deasy, who was arrested this side the Atlano!: with dynamite bombs in his possession, is said not to hari known the contents of the parcels, McDermott having 105..`e his passage and entrapped him. Phelan declared es occasion that could he manage to come across McDennfe before he left the country he would make it as " but or McDermott as O'Donnell did for Carey,"

And as surplus birds will be in the road when the chickens begin to appear, as well as eating their heads off now, their room will be much better than their company. - -.-- - MESSAGE FROM KHARTOUM. From General Lord Wolz4ley :—" Kora, 11th JanuarY, 1885, 1-50 p.m.—Messenger who left this on 18th December With letter to Gordon has just returned. He was one day in Khartoum, and left on the 28th December. He was taken Prisoner returning, and Gordon's letter taken from him. He bears marks of having been bound and beaten. town up in the clothes not taken from him was a fac-simile of the jsre- Vious little note bearing the came date, 'l4th December,' and announcing all well then. Gordon was in perfect health, and troops on the five steamers he saw were well and happy. The steamers seize cattle and grain, and take them up the river to Khartoum. The messenger re:urned on foot via J3aYads.." KORTI, SUNDAY.—A messenger has arrived from Khan- -I°llm. lie has p,rforrned the journey very rapidly, as he °My left here with a message from Lord Wolseley to General Gordon. on the 18th of December. He got through without Misadventure, but on his way back he was s:outpe.d and robbed by some tribesmen. General Gordon reports that all la well at Khartoum. His steamers ply without any serious interruption down to Metimmeh and bring in supplies. It is arranged that as soon ao General htewart's column 1 reaches Metammeh, Colonel Wilson, with three other officers, shall go up immediately in one of General Gordon's steamers 13 Khartoum, ascertain from him the exact position of affairs, and after consultation with the Gcner II as to the ,hest course to be pursued, return to Metammeh by steamer. 'Lhe Mudir of Dongola has arrived. He has hod a long interview with Lord Wolseley, and will, I believe, ao on to Merawi. Colonel Burnaby arrived on Friday, and went on yesterday to join General Stewart's cslumn at Crakdul.— Standard. LORD WOLSELEY'S ADVANCE. MEnawt, MONDAY —A wing of the Black Watch arrived “i'claY. All is going well with the Nile flotilla, under General Earle. From inquiries made in well-informed quarters in London, ,_°ll Tuesday evening, there is reason to believe that Lord wolseley will not advance with the headquarters staff until after the occupation of Metaameh, opposite Sheirley. Sir Herbert Stewart will take s'eps for opening up communica- tions with General Gordon at Khartoum. Ast otement pub- lished on Tuesday evening, that General Stewart's brigade Will remain at Matamneh until the arrival of General Earle's division, at the end of February, is regarded as en tirelv speculative. CAIRO TUESDAY. After reaching Metenneh, Generel Stewart's brigade will probably open communic itions with Khartoum, but will not push on to that place until the arri- N'al of General Earle, who is expected at Metemneh at the end of February, after taking Berber. I.IAMDAB, VIA MERAWI, TituasnAv, 6-25 P II —Reinforce- ments from Berber have arrived at Wady Gamr. The enemy say they will resist at Birteb. EGYPTIAN FINANCE. PROPOSALS OF FRANCE. The Ihrlin correspondent of the Pall Hall Gazette tele- graphs that he hears on unimpeachab!e authority that Ger- -,,,niutuY has derided to reject the proposals submitted by the vonglish Government for the settlement of Egyptian finance. 't is undeostood that Germany decided on Wednesday to accept the counter-proposals of the French Cabinet. Franca ,requires that the atnouttt of the new loan guaranteed by oogland shall be fixed at £9,000,000 instead of £5,000,000, order that the whole expenditure may be jrcvided for at one blow. 2 France insists upon separation of tha Daira Sanieh from the Domains, and declines to allow the re venue from these sources to be paid into the Bank of Eng- land. 3. WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. An adjourned meeting of this Council was held in the uncil Chamber at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of the Mayor (Alderman Harrison). There were also present Aldqrmen Holmes, Burgess, Chand- Ly, Webs'er ; Councillors Broadbent, Dixon, Fraucomb, Roberts, Burgess, Bolton, Wright. Hutchinson, Ashton, Barker, Dakin, Fleming, Greening, Marsh, and W. Pier. point ; Messrs. Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clera), Chorley (borough treasurer), and Longdin (borough surveyor).

THE BYE•LAWS. The MAYOR proposed, and Councilhr BROADBENT seconded the a doptioa of the minutes of the Watch Com- mittee, which recmmended for approval a number of draft bye-laws. It was thereupon decided to discuss the bye- laws seriatim, and for that purpose the standing orders were suspended, and the Council resolved itself into com- mittee.

JUVENILE EINWKING. Councillor MACKIE said that bye-law NO. 7—" No child under the age of ten years shall sell or offer for sale any article whatsoever in any street within the borough "—in- troduced something that would sound strange in the ears of many, and would act painfully in the case of large families. He thought that it was indeed stringent to go to a family where there might be three or four children under ten years of agehend say that not one of them was to earn even the smallaTt partion of his living, and at the same time that he must be sent to some public school. Those of them who were connected with the committee for paying ach el fees would know that there were constantly being brought beforej the committee women with a number of children. It was al question whether the age of ten years was not a great deal ' too high, and whether they vere net setting an example to the people of Warrington of high-banded legislation, which obtrtated itself again and again as they went through the bye-laws. He suggested that the age should be reduced. Alderman HOLMEs thought that ten years was too high. He should be content were it reduced to nine. Councillor BURGESS said he should feel disposed to a Rime to the by-law as recommended- All children were now compelled to go to school, and the bye-law practically meant that they should not be allowed to sell in the streets alter school tours. He thought it was not desirable that chil- dren under ten should be permitted to go about the streets at night to sell after they had been working all day. Alderman WEBSTER: The bye-lewe of the School Alend- once Committee prevent employment of caildren under ten years of age. Alderman BURGESS thought that work in school was fagging enough for children of ten years of age' and tie did not think that they should be called upon to do anything more. He supported the proposal of the committee as being a sound one. Alderman CHANDLEY said that he should be disinclined to sanction any reduction of the yea's, for he thought that ten was quite young enough for children to be about the streets selling anything. He was sure that frequently their sympathies must have been aroused, for it was painful to see children of tender years selling newspapers in the streets, and it was a thing that should be got rid of entirely. The Tower CLERK said that the same system was adopted at Leicester and Nottingham, and, he believed, at Manches- ter and Liverpool. Councillor BRoADBENT said that the committee had no wish to introdace high-handed bye-laws, or meddlesome ones. When they considered the pitiable sights to be seen occasionally in the streets, of little boys and girls, wet, and shivering with the cold, selling various articles, they would ctserve the benefit of the bye-law. They were also guided by the rules of the Educational Department, which provided that children tin ler ten years of age were not available for work, even as half timers. Councillor Macros then proposed, and Councillor DIXON seconded, that iastead of the word 'ten" be substituted the word "nine." The amendment, on being put to the meeting, was lost, and tee bye-law was adop el in its original form. Councillor MACKIE asked if bye-law 8, which provided that no child under the age of 14 should sell or offer for sale any articles in auy street within the borougb, between nine o'clock in the evening and sunrise the following morn- ing (rein March to December' or between eight o'clock in the evening and sunrise the following morning from Sep- tember to March, was intended to prevent boys 14 years of age, being employed before nine o'clock in the morning in such work as selling or delivering newspapers ? Couecillor BABKER Does it include milk selling ? (Laughter). The MAYOR: The object ie to prevent them disturbing people in their Louses, and at thie time of the year people do not generally get up with the lark. Alderman WEBSTER asked whether the delivery of news- papers previously ordered weuld come under the bye- law ? Toe TOWN CLERIC : No, the intention is to prevent people who are not expected going to houses and knocking the doors at early hours of the rooming. The MAYOR, in answer to Councillor Bolton, said that there had been complaints to the police of people knock- ing at doors. Councillor ROBERTS thought that the bye-law would work hardly in the case of milk-dealers, who in addition to serving regular customers, very often made chance sales. Alderman WEBSTER If that case came before me I should say that was not offering for sale within the mean- ing of the bye-law. The bye-law was passed on the motion of Coancillor BARKER, seconded by Alderman HotatEs, with the altera- tion that the word " seven o'clock " be suksrituted for the word sunrise, from September to March. STREET PROCESSIONS: THE SALVATION ARMY. Bye-law No.ll read: No proceesion or assemblage of a noisy Or tumultuous character, shall take place any public street within the borough' which shall tend to the obstruc- tion or annoyance of the public using or residing in such street, or tend to cause or provoke a breach of the peace. Any person taking part in any such procession or assem- blages ehall be liable to the penalty hereinafter pre. vided. Councillor ROBERTS asked who was to decide whether a procession was or Was not likely to be noisy or tumultuous? There was no provision in the bye-laws as to such authority, and it seemed to him that at present the only-Pereon likely to be able to interfere in a proposed pro:Nation was the 'Quid Constable, and he thought that it would be very' undesir- able to make that gentlemen the arbitrator of each an im- portant matter. Supposing any body of people in Warring- ton wished to have a procession on a given day—(l Voce:: A torchlight procession)—who was to say whether or not 1 they should have it? The Towle CLERIC said that it was not a question of what wag going to happen. The bye-law appertained to what actually took place. No one could prevent a procession taking place, and it was only in the event of its being noisy or tumultuous that the bye-law would apply. Councillor ROBERTS put a different construction on the worde of the bye-law, "No procession of a noisy or tumul- tuous oharacter ehall take place." That he would a,rant, but in the second place it said "No procession shall take I place in a street which shall tend to the obstruction or annoyance of the people residing in such streets." It might not be tumultuous ant noisy, but still might for a time ouatruct those living in the streets, It seemed clear to him that the processions in connection with the Salvation Army, as they were at present conducted, decently and in order, were not after all onducted without a little obetruction in the streets and some little inconverrience to people residing in such streets It would be possible under that bye-law for the processions to be put a stop to. He objected to the Chief Coostable being permitted on his own authority to interfere with any procession that was proposed should take place. At present, it seemed to him that there was no pro- perly constituted and regularly appointed authority tv de- cide these matters. The MAWR said that there was no other authority than the police to deal with a question of that kind. If the police failed to deal with such affairs in a rational manner they would show that they were unfit for the position they hold. He thought the public had sufficient guarantee that the power possessed by the police would not be abused. COuncillOr ROBERTS : I have had experience within a short time rather to the contrary cf that, and I am mit pro- -11 • ared to submit any matter in which am interested or this character to the dictation Or arbitration of the chief con- stable of Warrington. The Mason: Are you prepared to define some other 'mode of dealing with it? Councillor ROBERTS: I am prepared to suggest that at any ratethose who are responsible, the magistrates of the boroargh, shall be the persons to whom cases of this kind can be referred. The Tows CLERK said that they must be, and the MAYOR remarked that they could not make magistrates into detec- tive officers. Alderman WEBSTER said that the Chief Constable had already the power, as it was his absolute duty to preserve order in the streets. Councillor ROBERTS: If the Chief Constable has the authority, why should this bye-law be framed in these words as submitted? It seems to me there is no necessity if the Chief Constable has already the power. Councillor MACKIE said that when be read lave-laws 11 and 13 (the latter of which 4eals with noisy nuisances), it struck him th there might be some truth in the assertion that on the first opportunity there was to he an attempt made to padlock the movemeMs of those zealots of the Salvation Army. Mr. Roberts had viewed the question from another aspect, and he (Dr. aleckie) could understand his meaning although be had no sympathy with the suspioion that the Chief Constable would not he found fitting for his work. At any rate, he bad always the Mayor to fall back upon, and the Mayor during the last year had given the Chief Constable all the support that he could possibly be in need of. 13ye.law 13, which must be read in connection with 11, said thst any person who should by shouting, sing- ing, brawlinz, or playioz upon any musical or noisy instru- ment, make a disterbance in or near any street, should be liable. He thought on readieg Each love-laws that an attempt was beirg made to bring the people down to a state Of the most perfect Buie= silence, not merely on Sundays, but every day of the week. Why should there .be any interference with the Salvation Army. Let them amg, said he, and God help them. He need to hear them as they passed and to wish thorn God speed, and he wished be could help them to some better instruments than they posseszed. These people were doing a vast amount of good in the town. He was once astonished and delighted at tbe warm way in which he heard the Chief Constable speak of their anceessful exertions

He found the Public Hall on Sundays crowded to the door with the best looking of our working-men, all respectably dressed, many with their wives and daughters, and tney pre- sented an appearance all would b 3 proud to see in any or- dinary place of warship. They , had a belief that every man had a day of grace, and that all that was wanted was to bring the men within the influence of the gospel minis- tration, and they were working in the back slams of the town, and in places where no clergymen were to be found except at the call of the sick and dying. They seem,- plished this with such a small amount of annoyance that it should willingly be borne with. Do not let them rouse up the feeling of that mass of people, for they,had risen to be the strongest religious body, minus the Es.ablished Church, and were sending men to every pert of the earth to "bring in "what they considered the outcast, and be hoped War- rington would not let itself be advertised all over ti.e country as trying at the eleventh hour to stop them, under the guise of keeping order in,the streets. Councillor ROBERTS explatabi that what he Said with reference to. the Chief Constable was said with no disrespect to that gentleman, and was not in any way meant to re- flect upon the manner in which he conducted his business. He thoaght it a mistake for any public servant to be placed ' in a possibility of being in =diet with any section of the inhabitants, Councillor BARKER then proposed that bye-law 11 be not confirmed, as it interfered with the liberty of the subject. Alderman BURGESS S2COElilt,'d the proposal. He thought that it was better that they did not meddle in the matter. There was, he thought, a great deal of truth in the remarks of Councillor Mackie regarding the object sought to be ob- tahyd—that the Salvation Army were to be interfered with, and their processions pet haps put a stop to. He did not t ink that was necessary. If they did legislate in that spirit it must be universal in its application, and if the Ai my was not allowed to walk on Sunday, how would they do on Walking Day, when the streets were filled by thousands of children, a beautiful sight, but nevertheless an obstracdou to traffic? All must be treated alike. Alderman HoLues said he should support the proposition of Councillor Barker. CouncilLr BURGESS said that the bye-law would not in- terfere with the Salvation Army any more than other people if they behaved themselves. LECFURES BY MR. lIOW.ES.
SPEECHES BY MR. W. CROSFIELD AND MR.
McNIINNIES, M.P.

In the course of the present week three very largely- attended lectures on political Voiles have been given in . Warrington, under the auspices of the Liberal Association, by Mr. Joseph Howes, of Leeds. On Monday evening the lecture was given in the Co-operative Hall, the subject be- ing: " The History of Toryism—a lesson and a waruing." The hall was completely filled. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. Crosfield (the Liberal candidate for Warringten), and there were also present Councillors C. Broadbent, H. Roberts, Fleming, Barker, and W. Pierpoint, Dr. Garman, Messrs, F, A. Roberts, R. Roberts, A. F. Browne, Bircball, Mounfield, and other. Toe Cnaiamew, who was greeted with loud applause, said :—Ladies and gentlemen, we have before us a large subject, and I know you have coins here to hear Mr. Howes rather than to hear me, and I judge that be will be very well able to occupy all the time you can spare him in the treatment of the subject which is laid out for him. He is going to tell us about the history of Toryism; its lemon and its warnings. Anyone of these three topics would well occupy an evening; and if Mr. Howes will kindly allow me a few minutes to speak of the hiatory of Toryism I shall be very glad to leave him the other two points of its lessons and its warnings. I find that our great historian, Lord Ma- caulay, speaking about Toryism in its commencement., which was 200 years ago—about 1680—points out whit will strike you as a very curious circumstance in connection with the phase of political opinion which the word Toryism conveys te our mind. Political feeling then, as now, ran very high. Parties were divided into very many sections, and amongst these were two sectioas which went by the name of the Birmingbams,and the anti-Birminghams. It was this latter party that Toryism supplanted. It is a curious thing, and shows us how political feeling remains in one locality, that we find Mrmingham is now the representative of anti-Toryism as it was in the day when Toryism origi- nated. (Applause.) The word Tory was first used as an insulting nick-name for a political party; and it is St tted to have t alien its rise from an Irish word which metres" give." It is said that when airy man who Was unwilling tee work for his own living, but preferred to live by other people's means, hid himself behind a hedge and burst forth upon sulitary travellers, with the cry of "Lorre !"—in other words, "deliver or die!" (teinglitsre I think you will recognise that Toryism has not to any very material degree altered in corns of its characteristic; up to the present day. (Hear, hsar, and applause.) In.lrish Acs of Parliament of that day Tor ice and robbers were classed together without any apparent feeling of incen- gruity. (L iughter and applause ) We have, h ee ever' be- come mere polite in the present day; and, although the characteristics of the Tories remain to some extent what they were then, we donut describe them in quite such rough language as our forefathers of 200 years age. You will remember .that a Minister speaking of those who were opposed to him in the House of Com- mons spoke of them on one occasion when they, with singular audacity. curried to a succeesfal issue the measures which t iey load opposed throughout a long series of years—measures which they carried as if they had al- ways been in accord wile them—that statesman spoke of them as having " caught our party bathing and stole our clothes." (Litiebtere Lord Derby, a distinguished repre- sentative of the Tory party, had evidently much the some feeling with regard to his own party, for when on one occe- glen they had very successfully acco:npliseed a similar sort of thing, Lord Derby spoke of it as "dishing the Whigs." It described, at any rate, the transference of whatever pro- perty there might be in political measares from one party to another. The word Tory, we think, is going out of use. We certainly have a slight remembrance of it left to us still in the epithet or description which our opponents are trying to give themselves, that of "Tory Democracy "—(laughter) —a phrase which seems quite as easy to nee to understand as would be the recital from a sailor of his encountering an east west wind. (Laughter.) But the spirit of Toryism still survives. I find that Dr. Johnson explains that the word" Tory" describes "one who adheres to the ancient constitution, the apostolic hierarchy, and the Church of England." What Toryism was in Dr. Johnson's day it still remains in oar day. Another distinguished Tory, who was one of the eailieat to ally himself to the Tory party—Lord Bolingbroke—giving some of the peculiarities or ideas as- sociated with Toryism enumerates, among others, the fol- lowing :—"Divine, hereditary, indefeasible right, passive obedience, prerogative, non-resistance, and slavery." (Laughter and applauds.) Malay others lee gives which have ps.ssed away with past hietory,and are with us no mere, and therefore can no longer belong even to the Tory ports, ; but these in their essence, still continue; and the old Tories ' what few of them remain still adhere to these ideas, and the spirit of Toryism, I say, still remains with us. ` NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION: A Conference promoted by the National Liberal Federa- tion was held on Wednesday. at Ipswich, under the preci• dency of Alderman W. Kendrick, of Birmingham. The Chairman said that in the recent agitation their work had been mainly in the large centres of population but now that the franchise had been extended they would devote their r energies to the instruction and organisation of the agricul- total labourers, who would have a large voicelin the election of the new Parliament—Mr. Celman, M P., moved a revs- lution cont,ratulsting the Government upon their success in passiqg the Franchise Bill and in securing the promise of a Radical and comprehensivemeasure of redistribution. —Mr. Richard Chamberlain, who foresaw many advantages from the single-member proposal, seconded the resolution, and it was carried.—The Rev. T. W. Fowler, rector of Min, submitted a proposal in favour of applying the principle of popular representation to the local government of counties. Re was in favour of village councils as splins+. vestries, and thought the creation of an elective body in each rural dis- trict would awaken the political intelligence of the people. Tke resolution was adopted, as was another calling for a reform in the system of land tenure.—The Rev. J. F. A. Hervey (Ipswich) asked the Conference to pass a resolution approving the substitution of an affirmation for the Parlia- mentary oath, which was agreed to, and the proceedings terminated.

In the evening the Right Hon. Joe. Chamberlain ad- dressed a crowded meeting in the Ipswich Corn Exchange. He said the recent settlement had fulfided their most san- guine expectations. The. Franchise Act and the State Dill conatituted a transfer of power which was absolutely -un- paralleled in the history of political reform. For geed or for evil, Democracy had established itself in the seat of authority, and the Government of the many would be sub- stituted for the Government of the few." The Liberal pre. gramme would have to be enlarged and party methods must be altered in view of the new electoral power thus created. In reference to his recent remarks at Birmingham on the dirties of property, which have been widely and severely criticised, Mr. Chamberlain said he believed that the danger to property lay in its abuse, and that the interest of the rich would be found to consist in a generous interpretatien of their obligations and in a full and free Acknowledgment of the rights of the poor: He repudiated the contentione cf the Times that there were no rights outside those created by laws, for in tint case, as the majority made the laws, it could, without regard to considerations of natural justice and equity, secure is own interest at the expense et the minority. If the rich wanted their rights to be respected as they ought to be they were bound in turn to respect the rights of their less fortunate brethren. Without attempting to dictate the Liberal policy, he ventured to assert that in future they would have to give a good deal more attention to what was called social legislation. Education.harl been made compulsory, but he hoped one of their lirst efforts would be to make it free. The first work of a new Neje- ,' ment, if the present Government remained in power, would be to provide local government for the counties. The greatest needs of our time were the provision of healthy de- cent dwllings in large towns at fair rents, and in the cowls- ! try facilities for the labourer to obtain a small plot of land. The incidence of taxation, and particularly income tix. re- spired readjustment, and our land laws needed overhauling. tie expressed Lis sympathy with the distressed agricultur- ists of this country, but warned them arzainet expecting relief from Mr. Lowther's scheme of taxing imported corn. The moat hopeful method of reviving tnat indu,try was to go hick to the old plan of multiplied freeholders—the pea sante and yeomen, who were the namt independent and com- fortable class in the community. That could not be done a. once, but he said they were bound to do all in their powert to stimulate by all kinds of legislation what was a matter of essential importance if English agriculture was ever again to hold its own. A hearty vo'e of thanks was accor- ded to the right hon. gentlemau, who, dnring the deli- very of his speech, was suffering acutely from neuralgic pains.

NEW BOOKS, &c. 4 .4 Bib and Tucker " (Messrs. Sampson, Low, Marston, Searle, and Rivingtoa, London,) is a very clever little work, by Elsa D'Esterre-Keeling. It purports to be " the revela- tions of an infant in arms "—life being viewed from the peculiar stand-point of el very precocious" chick." Every chapter is racily written ; there is great variety of incident, and yet there is nothing but what might come within an infant's purview—once assuming " the little beggar " to be capable of "taking it all in." The beok ought to have a good sale; it. is capital reading. " Text and Verse for Every Day in the Year," published by the same firm, is a series of scripture passages and parallel selec ions from the writings of the American poet, Jahn Grenleaf Whittier, arranged by Gertrude W. Cartland. It is a long way above the average of this class of works, as it has the merit of not being too " goody-goody." Whittier's writings lend them- selves with singular facility to an arrangement of this kind. The passages given are for the most part complete in thetn• selves, and, as they are powerful as well as full of religious feeling, they will stimulate interest in the poet's works, which are too little known on this side of the Atlantic. "Illustrated Temperance Anecdotes" (S. W. Partridge and Co., London), forms a second series of facts and figures for the platform and the people. It is compiled by the editor of the "British Workualn" who has done his work well. The illustrations are numerous and strikinge the letter press is very superior, and the tales are very read- able. As the cost (in cloth) is one shilling only, the Wok should be in the hinds of all advoc nes of temperance. We had eocasioa last week to refer to and c immend "War and its Consequences," by Profeseor Leone Levi ; also issued as one of Messrs. Partridge and Co.'s shilling books. No phase of the question is over-looked, in being considered econo- mically, commercially, financially and morally. The" Magazine of Art" for January (Messrs. Cassell and Co.) has for its frontispiece a charming re-production of the portrait of Lady Maria Weldegrave, the original being by John Downman, A R.A. Continuing " Artie's' Homes," we have now Mr. Pettie's at Hampstead. The interiors, as revealed by illustration and text, are thoroughly character- istic of the painter. There are two very fine plates of the French actor M. Coqueliu, and more interesting still are the Illustrations to the article on" Pompeii in Black and White." There is an appreciative sketch of the career and work of Either Vedder, the artist, with specimens of his style. Mr. W. Archer contributes some lively verse; following which there is "A round in France' (illustrated) the number con- cluding with a valuable review of Linton's warke on wood engraving. Cassell's fine-art edition' of Longfellow reaches part 5. The frontispiece is a fine engraving illustrating the lines "And the Moon rose o'er the city, behind the dark church tower." There are illustrations to several of the songs. and we have the beginning of " Evangeline," which promises to prove a treat pictorially as it is poetically. " Cassell's Family Magazine " for J multi?, commences the year well. The plates are numerous and some of them very striking—particularly that of the young lady who is "lacing the weed in a new character," and that of "Reu- ben Sparrow." Amongst the more noteworthy articles are —Our Autograph Books, Clear Soups, How Repousse- work is Done, How I furnished for £1.90, and Sir Richard Owen and His Work. Fiction holds its place, the Model Riding Club promises well, and the Gatherer is es- pecially interesting. The frontispiece to this month's Quiver is'. a palpable hit." It is the head of a young girl; the expression on the face is that of faith, and as a picture 1 ills perfect in its way. There is a pretty view of Wycliffe ' Church along with a short piper entitled "In Wycliffe Land," which will be re ad pest now with interest. The Bishop of Bath and Wells contributes " Thouehte for the Coming Year"; Dr. Bsn tr a paper on "The Marks of the , Lord Jesus"; Dr. Bryan one on "Popular American Preachers"; and there are other interesting articles and stories. Girls and boys who have not been in the habit of , taking in "Little Folks" may now with advantage make , acquaintance with the migizine, the twenty-firet , volume being commenced with the present issue. Ihe new . Ifeatures are very numerous, and all of them are attractive, "Old Merry" being to the fore avith " Legends and stories of famous rivers." "Three Little Kittens" is the name given to , the first illustration, which is in colours, and very pretty. 1" Cassell's Popular Gardening" (part 9) continues the article . on " the decorative use of flowers," with a tasteful and sug- gestive illustration, and there are articles on common gar- den flowers, the propogation and cultivation of the pine apple, hardy fruits, glass structures and appliances, &e. " The Book of Health " loses none of its interest. The Brain, in the currenlissue, is treated of at length, including its quality, elaborititn of structure balance of parts, func- tional habits, flood supply, sac. There is a valuable chapter, too, on sleep, and education in relation to the nervous system. " The Encyclopedic Dictionary (part 12) con- cludes the letter B and cornmencss C. The more we sae of the great work and the more we are assured that it will be invaluable, not only to students and literary men, but to readers of every class. "The English Illustrated Magazine" for January is "a good average" number. There is an excellent article on " Shakespeare's Coutitry," with some suitable illustrations ; but the leading piper is a "Calvados" in Normandy, Some of the illustrations to which (by W. J. Hennessy) are very flue. "The Dramatic Out-look," which is to be continued, is well written, and fiction is strong with "The Girl at the Gate" by Wilkie Collins, and "A Family Affair " by Hugh Conway. Part 2of "Ward and Lock's Technical Journal and ludustrial Self Instructor "is to hand It is destined to ! become of great value, making as it does for good workmanship on the most intelligent lines. There is some- thicg for everybody who has work to do. The wide ranee of the present part may be c mcieved when we say there are special articles (illustrated) on the joiner, the carpenter, the bricklayer, the road-maker, the calico printer, and the orna- mental draughtsman, while the alkali maker, the cotton worker, and the grazier and cattle breeder are not forgotten. We have also received "Le Moniteur de la Mode" (Is.). ‘• Mera's Journal " (a), " Myra's Threepenny Journal," all published by Myra and Son (late Gouband and Son); and " The Season" (1s). These fashion journals give the fair reader plenty of choice, and they are very attractive with their numerous plates and patterns.

It has all along been discouraged by the Queen. The Princess has DO money, but the usual 5001 given to sons and daughters of the Queen on their marriage Wilk be voted to the Princess Beatrice by Parliament. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JANUARY 17, 1855.

GERMANY is now finding that, even in the matter of colonial extension, it is not all gold that glitters ; the roses are attractive, but when they come to be grasped it is found that there are thorns amongst them. Prince BISMARCK has had his way in annexing the northern part of New Guinea, and there can be no question that the move he has made has pleased his countrymen. He was pre- pared to run the risk of irritating England; but he does not seem to have been prepared for being irritated in return. And yet he is Irritated; and he took no pains to conceal the fact in the important speeches which he made in the Reichstag on Saturday. He has had occasion to complain of the conduct of British representatives at Cameroons, a Get man settlement in West Africa, in inciting insurrection amongst the natives. But he admits that from the extent of the colonial possessions of Great Britain, it is difficult to " exercise everywhere a strict control over men and circumstances, even over its own officials." Admitting this, he will come to see that Germany may in time have troubles of her own through the mistaken zeal of men who are now being set to work to carry out the policy of colonial extension. Earl GRAN- viLLE has promised to make inquiries on the subject of the dispute, and to do what he can to bring about a better understanding be- tween the English and Germans at Carneroons. Meantime, Prince BISMARCK has got author- ity to build a steamer for coasting in that part of the world, and when built it will, of course, have to be paid for. Dr. WIND - THORST, who spoke later, referred to Ger - many as being surrounded either by enemies or envious powers; and this brought the German Chancellor on his feet again. He repudiated the idea that Germany was not on good terms with all the European Powers; and revealed how carefully he is nursing France by saying that Germany now stood on a better footing with her than she had at any time since r 866. Coming to existing relations with England, he said: —"That England, in the consciousness that Britannia rules the waves, should open her eyes with astonishment when her cousin the land rat, as we appear to be in English eyes, suddenly also sails out to sea, is not to be wondered at; yet this feeling of astonishment is in no wise shared by the highest, the ruling circles in England." This pregnant obser- vation, uttered with characteristic force, is one which may with advantage be pondered by the Jingoes of this country. They are the people who have been "astonished," and who have so far looked upon it as an offence that Germany should "sail out to sea " that they have been loud in their denunciation of Lord DERBY in particular in that he has not —in some way not of course explained—put a stop to the proceeding. With regard to the suggested possibility of an armed conflict with England, Prince BISMARCK was em- phatic in repudiating the suggestion. He reminded the Reichstag that Germany and England had not been at war since iBo6 ;

and, he added, "According to my dipl matic experience, I can see no grounds of a possible breach between us and England?' This is very reassuring, as showing that Ger- many knows herself and her surroundings too well to be desirous of picking a quarrel with England, and yet it is not to be inferred that, there are no causes of difference—that Prince BISMARCK is carrying all before him, and that he is therefore wholly happy. Germany has annexed a portion of New Guinea, and no sooner has she done so than there is news of opposition on the part of the natives, who may be supposed to have some interest in the matter. Then again, it is stated that, by way of counter-move, the autho:ities of New Zealand have intimated their intention of annexing the Samoa Islands. It is, in fact, stated that there is a steamer ready to start on this mission the moment sanction to the proposal is received from Lord , DERBY. What makes this intelligence trying to Prince BISMARCK is the fact , that Germany has got a good footing in Samoa, and that in this case it is asserted that , the natives are demanding annexation on the • part of England! No wonder he should say —" it is a remarkable coincidence, this re- sistance of the natives against German occu- pation on the various coasts." What he means is that this resistance is the work Of , Englishmen, if not of Eneland ; and we are by no means sorry that he should be driven '. to the conclusion that annexation involves vexation. He is finding that two can play at a game of cross-purposes, and that he is not • by any means as powerful in Southern Seas as he is in Germany. Not that we would have the COLONIAL SECRETARY sanction the , annexation of Samoa, especially if, as alleged, there is an understanding with Germany that the independence of the islands should be preserved. It is not for England to be scared because Germany has taken to colonising ; or to go careering the seas in search ef islands to annex. We have already incurred vast responsibilities in every part of the world, and we must be careful not to add to those responsibilities without the most care- ful consideration of all the issues which InnY be involved. We are glad to think that Lord DERBY in such matters is the man to act soberly and wisely. He is not to be led .h astray by a momentary impulse ; and has, happily, nothing whatever about him of the charlatanry which would annex a Cyprus with no other object than that of " splitting the ears of the groundlings." He has bee!ll subjected to not a little abuse because he din not anticipate Germany in New Guinea, but Germany is already discovering that she is in trouble with the natives. In fact, judging from the tone of the German CHANCELLOR'S remarks, it would seem that he is by n° means proud of his latest stroke of polici• He can see that he has nothing to gain permitting the relations between England an'.' Germany to become strained, and his speeches on Saturday were a tribute in their waY t° the power of England and to her prstige under the present Administration.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF I:IOPF,RUNCOEN.—The fortnightly meeting was held on Thursday evening, under the presidency Of Mr. W. Shaw,. of the Mersey Missions to Seamen. An excellent programme was gone through, and an address was delivered by Mr. J. Ashley. BETHESDA MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS, RUNCORN.— Mr. Walter Millington read a paper on " The People's Land" before the members of this society on Wednesday evening. An interesting discuseion ensued. WIDNES C.E.T.B.—At the weekly meeting, on Thursday, Mr. J. Foleyr the lay reader at the Parish Church, delivered a lecture on" London and its outcasts" to a large audience. A musical entertainment was also given, and Mr. T. Ather- ton presided. SLEEPING OUT AT Wintens.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Martin Gibbons and Martin Dunn were each sen- tenced to seven days' hard labour for sleeping on the works of the Widnes Alkali Company on Saturday night.—On Wednesday, for a similar offence, committed on Tuesday night, John Flynn was sent to gaol for seven days. THE DISAPPEARANCE OF AN OLD MAN AT RUNCORN.— The body of Jonathan Rushton (80), Shancross-row, Hal- ton-road, was found in the Old Quay Canal at Runcorn, on Thursday morning. He had been missing since the 10th December, and the body when recovered was much decem- ber. Yesterday, Mr. T. J. Ridgway, the Coroner, held an ingnest on the body at the Burial Board Offices, and a ver- dict of "Found drowned" was returned. WIDNES AND THE REDISTRIBUTION there—The inhabi- tants of several townships in the district sutrounding Wid- nes are making efforts to become the centre of a new elec- toral division under the Redistribution Bill. Crarston, Wavertree, and Prescot are foremost in this contest Widnes people, however, think their claims to the honour are pre-eminent. They maintain that the townships men- tioned above do not approach Widnes in industrial impor- tance, and are thoroughly convinced that if their claims receive deserved consideration Widnes will have the distinc- tion of returning a member under tha new act. WIDNES AND THE Sinn CANAL —On Thursday a deputa- tion from the Widnes Local Board had an interview with the Mersey Dock and Harbour Board in respect to their proposed opposition to the Ship Canal scheme, on the ground that if carried out as suggested there will be great danger of the approaches to docks and the canal becoming blocked up. No definite conclusion was arrived at as to whether this Board would join Widnes in opposing the bill. There is, however, a strong impression afloat that the Mersey Dock and Harbour Board will appear as the oppo- nents of the bill when it comes before Committee. The Earl and Countess Granville concluded their visit to the Queen at Osborne yesterday morning, and crossed to. Portsmouth, leaving for the Victoria station by the 11,10 ordinary train.

SINGULAR CASE OF EXTORTION.—At Chester, on Thar. day, Jane Hughes was charged with making a false declara- tion of birth. The prisoner bad been living with a gentle- man in Dumfries, and in September last she informed him that a child had been born at Chester, where she made the usual declaration to the registrar. By threats of exposure she obtained money from the gentleman, who afterwards discovered that the prisoner's statement regarding the birth k was untrue. She was fined 50s and costs.

Mr. Burt adelressed a meeting of his constituents at Blyth on Wednesday night. He expressed satitfa-tion, on the whole, with the Seats Bill, and recommended that the principle of proportional representation should be discussed on its merits, but thought the adoption of a LSecond ballot" would be the better way out of the difficulty. div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY. JAMTARY 171, 1885:

CHOIR PARTY AT RUNCORN. The choir of the Primi- tive Methodist Chapel, Crreenway-road, had their annual party on Tuesday, and spent a very pleasant evening. DRUNKENNESS AT WIDNES.—At the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, the following persons were each tined for drunkenness :—Wm. Winters, Bernard Kilcoin,.Wm. Burns, Ann Dogherty, Wen. Toan, and Robert Norman.—On Wed- nesday tines wee imposed upon the following for like of- fence :—John Wright, Emmanuel Smith, Catherine Lavin, Patrick Kennedy, Alice Keating, and John Fandy. RAFFLING AT BAZAARS.—The Rochdale Corporation Watch Committee have instructed the Tewn Clerk to issue notices against raffling at bazaars, warning all persons of their illegality, and that the law will be strictly enforced to prevent them. The committee has also decided to call the attention of bakers to the law as it affects their trade, that they are bound to weigh bread in the presence of the

WIDNES- SCHOOL BOAR.D, PROSECUTION.—Mr. G. H. Danby, at the instance of the School Boardournmoned the following Persons to Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday to answer a charge of neglecting_ to send their children regularly to school :—John Burns, John Kinsella, John Martin, Patrick Lynch, Margaret Carr, Patrick Foy,. John Bowyer, Sarah A. Bradley, John Muiharkey, Jas. Stanton,. Walter Allen, and Robert IL ey. The cases were proved, and the usual penalties of 58 inflicted. MAGIC LANTERN ENTERTAINMENT AT EIINCORN.—OR Thursday evening Mr. Annett, head master at Holy Trinity School, gave a magic lantern entertainment to the scholars of his schddl who were in regular atti-ndance. The irregu• lara bad to pay a small charge. The subject illustrated was "Central Africa," and the admirable representations thrown on the screen proved highly interesting to the children. On Thursday next the Bishop of Chester will distribute the prize to the scholars in the Public Hall.

purchaser. FATAL ICE ACCIDENT.— Edward Wm. Clemea ta son of Peter Clemeau, engine-driver, Warrington, was drowned whilst on a frozen pit at Sutton on Wednesday. The boy was on a visit to his grandfather, who warned him not to venture on the ice. As he was absent from the house longer than usual, search was made for him, and near a hole in the centre of the ice on the pit the boy's cap was found, and shortly afterwards his dead body was recovered from the water. Castors BARCLAY.—The Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., vicar of Runcorn, has, it is stated, resigned the office of rural dean of Frodeharn, in consequence of increasing years and declining health. It is understood that the Bishop of Chester has off.ired the position to the Rev. Canon Greenall, M.A., rector of St. Wilfred's Church, Grappen- hall. On inquiry yesterday, our representative was informed that the condition of the Rev. Canon Barclay bad greatly improved during the past week, and there were strong hopes held out of his ultimate recovery. Sympathetic references to the rev. gentleman were made yesterday atean adjourned meeting of the school Board, and also at the annual meet- ing of the Savings' Bank. TRADE PROSPECIS —We are glad to find that the view expressed in these columns, that the coming year bears is more promising aspect than that which is behind us, is shared by men of business. Messrs. J. C. Monnsey and Co , ef '7, Laurence Pountney Hill, 8.C., state at the close of their review of the past year that, in looking forward to the future, they take encouragement from the fact that prices have now reached the earns level as in 1879 w when BO much depression existed, and it, therefore, seems impos- sible for any further decline to take place. Many large buyers evidently take the some view, as there certainly is more disposition in some quartets to take advantage of present rates to cover r,quirements for the next six months. Should any extra demand set in during the early nionths of the year, prices are altnost certain to rebound, as it requires very little to inspire sufficient confidence to bring about a general improvement in trade.—lran. A HEARTLESS HUSBAND AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, James Ciregson, a young man, Was charged that he being an able bodied person able to work did neglect to maintain his wife and children, who became chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Utrion.—Mr Scannell stated that the prisoner for a considerable time past had consistently neglected to maintain his wife and three children. The eldest child was five years of age, and the youngest two weeks. The family were admitted to the Workhouse on the 15. h December, but about a fortnight previously the woman had an interview with her husband at Warrington. He then informed her that he would do nothing for her unless he were compelled, although at this time he was employed by Mr. Isherwood and in receipt of 22s per week. In consequence of the prisoner's bad conduct his employer discharged him. Instead of going into respect- able lodgings he preferred to sleep in barns and outhouses. There was £3 68 6d due to the Union. The Bench sentenced the prisoner to a month's hard labour. PANTOMIME AT THE ALEXANDRA THEATRE, LIVERPOOL. —lt will he seen from our advertising columns that Mrs. Edward Baker, the enterprising lessee of the Royal Alex- andra Theatre, Liverpool, is this season treating her patrons to a pantomime under the title of "Aladdin." Following upen an undoubted success the previous Christmas, the pantomime is one which we should think not excelled, if even equalled, for spectaculargrandeur and sparkling music, ' by anything of its kind in the provinces. The enthralling story from the Arabian Nights has been put upon the stags in a manner which realises all of the gorgeousness and bril- liance which it suggests to the most fanciful mind. The scenic effects are of a high order of merit, notably "the haunt of the storm witches" and 'cave of jewels." There is a splendidly-arranged procession representing the towns of:Lencashire, and a grand ballet of the Months lead- ing up to a transformation scene of dazzling brilliance and colour. The music is vivacious and tuneful, the topical and other songs smart and humonrous, and the dialogue racy and unflagging in interest. We can confidently recommend a visit now that the railways afford special facilities for attending the pantomime. Knowles, NV. Wilkinson, J. Mclntyre, T. J. Rigby, W. Bradford, T. Bennett, T. G. Rigby, Derbyshire, H. Houghton, P. Ticks, T. Baguley, C. T. Whitley, T. Bate, Barber, J. Farmers had hard times at pre- sent, and if the rates could be reduced a little it would be a very good thing.—The Clerk read correspondence relating to the escape of water from the canal at Walton and Stock- ton Heath, and a committee was appointed to consider the question.—The Clerk reported that no clauses prejudicial to the interests of the Board had been inserted in the Man- chester Ship Canal Bill —Reports as to the condition of various roads in the district were approved, and Mr. Ken' worthy drew attention to the fact that a quantity of soil had been removed from footpaths. The Surveyor was in- structed to inquire into the matter and report.—There was no other business of interest. Mearcruseren SHIP CANAL: TILE PARLIAMENTARY DE- Posrr.—The sum, £296,293, necessary to comply with the Standing Orders in the case of the Ship Canal Bill, was on Tuesday deposited in the Bank of England. The amount is equal to 4 per cent. upon £6,835,6A the parliamentary V estimate for the canal, dock works, and roads; and 5 per cent. open £457,292, the estimate for substituted railways— a total of £7,292,972, which is the official estimate of the cost of the works proposed to he carried nut under the bill. The deposit it required to show that the promoters are in earnest with regard to the undertaking, and as this is the third occasion on which they have provided so large a sem, ills fair to infer that they are serious. The Weekly meet- ing of the Provisional Committee was held in the Board- room, 704 Market-street, Manchester, yesterday afternoon, and in the absence of Mr. Adamson, Dr. Mackie was voted to the chair. A. resolution, passed by the Corporation of Oldham in favour of the canal project, was submitted and received with great satisfaction. It was reported that the bill would be before the Examiner on Standing Orders on Wednesday next, and will probably be referred to a Select Committee early in March. The prepaTations for next ses- sion are being pushed foraeard with all possible vigour, and all will be in readiness by the time the bill comes on for in- quiry. MR. W. CROSFIELD AT TUE BANQUET TO Mr. FOWLER. —Mr. H. 11. Fowler, the Under Secretary for the Home De- partment, was entertained at a banquet on .Wednesday night given by the Liverpool Reform Club. In responding to the toast of his health he expressed his belief that the Government would pursue to the end the policy on which it came into office, and that if an appeal could be made to the country now that policy would he endorsed. Mr. William Crosfield, J.P., the Liberal candidate for Warring- ton, in proposing the toast of "The Houses of Parliament," said that in 008 House there was too little energy to do any great thing, and its the other there was too much energy in opposing things we desired to see accomplished. He took it, however, that the next House of Commons, taken in a mass rather than in any individual sense, would be com- posed of men who were more inclined to businese, and who would see that business accomplished to a much greater amount than in the past. Mr. Fowler had pointed out some of the elements which dragged upon the legislative machinery, and they hoped that in the next Parliament many of these elements would altogether disappear. (Ap- plause.) With regard to the House of Commons, from what he knew of it, it contemplated an early visit to the country. There was every reason to hope that it would return from that visit in a much better state of body and mind in which to perform the duties which the electors of England imposed upon them. (Cheers.) TIIE REV. CHARLES GARRETT ON THE EARLESTOWS TEMPERANCE DISCUSSION.—The discussion on the temper- ate or intemperate remarks of a certain rev, gentleman, at Earlestown, has occasioned some interest in the neighbour- hood. One of the writers made a statement to the effect that "the Rev. Charles Garrett was supported in the con. ference by the moderate men on condition that he would not make total abstinence a paramount consideration, and that he would allow a certain latitude in the advocacy of temperance and it was through the support of the moder- ate party that Mr. Garrett was elected president of the con- ference.' On seeing this statement a correspondent forwar- ded a copy of the paper to the Rev. Charles Garrett. ex- president of the Wesleyan Conference, and the follow- ing reply has been received from that gentleman: "Liverpool, January 14th. Many thanks for the papers so kindly sent. The letter of A Disgusted Moderator ' is evidently written by someone who knows nothing of Wesleyan Methodism. Mast certainly it would be something new under the sun for anyone to talk to either of our brethren about 'a condition' on which he should be elected Presi- dent of the Conference. Such a thing is simply out of the question. You are therefore quite at liberty to say that the statement that a condition was named to me either directly or indirectly is absolutely untrue. No one ever asked me to be President and therefore, of course, a condition could not have been named. Had anyone been foolish enough to have done such a thing I should have regarded it as an insult and have acted accordingly,—l am, yours truly, CHARLES Gemara."

Wright, that he was of opinion that an inquiry would trive to be held before the sewer was constructed.—Mr. Wright suggested the propriety of dealing with the Lugsil dale district at the same time. PROPOSED INCORPORATION OF THE TOWN.-Dr. O'Keeffe moved that the clerk be instructed to write to various towns that had recently received charters of incorporation, in order to ascertain what benefits these towns derived from incorporation in order that the Board might have full in- formation before they took steps for having Widnes incir- p.rated.— Mr. Webster seconded the proposition. —The Chairman thought the chief advantage was that they could borrow cheaper.—Dr. O'Keeff observed that if no advantages were derived they might as well remain as they were and better. (Hear. hear.)—Carried. This concluded the business.
