The employmeet of the men was not, as Mr. Wright had suggested, a matter of charity, which the Board had no right to consider, and if the money were Maid the committee would simply have exceeded the amount of their estimate.—Mr. Gaskell proposed, and Mr. Carey seconded an amendment in favour of the consideration of the subject being deferred.—The amendment was put, and four voted for it and eight against it.—Mr. Midwood then pro- posed, and Mr. Dutton 'seconded, a special resolution con- firming the minutes.—Mr.Carey spoke strongly against the ',roposition, end proposed an amendment that the considera- ,, ion of the matter bedeferrel.—Mr. Gaskell seconded Mr. c arey'e amendment, and said the public works recommended to be carried, out were totally unnecessay. He did not see how the money could be obtained without a special appli- cation to the Local Government Board. The proposal of the committee hnd been " sprung " upon the Board, and he, for one, would never sign a cheque for the money.—me Midwood's motion was carried by ,eight to four votes. A COMMITTEE ON STRIKE.—Mr Sadler moved, and Mr. Hougton seconded the adoption of the minutes of the Hos- pital Committee, which centained no item of special interest. '---Mr. Webster asked how long Mr. Midwood had been a member of the committee.—Mr. Sadler explained that the members of the committee had been on strike for several months, and he bad been compelled to call in outside help. —Mr. Houghton said he felt nqwell on the day of the meeting, and therefore did not attend.—Mr. Midwood con- eidered it a hardship that as be was the only member of the Board who occupied a position on five committees he should be called upon to do the work of others. (Hear, hear.) -The members of the Board ought to attend to their duties. (Hear, hear.)--The minutes were adopted. I SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.—THE VENTILATING LAMPS.— ' The minutes of the Sewerage Committee contained letters, 16th December and 2nd January, from Fawkes Brothers, asking that the question of their claim be reconsidered, and stating that they have kept the surface of the roads in re- pair over six months. The committee recommended that the question be not reopened, and that notice be given Fawkes Brothers that they are liable for the maintenance of the road for six months from date of final certificate.— The Clerk had reported that the Highway Committee re- : fuse to be responsible for the lighting of the ventilating lamps until they were re-arranged for lighting purposes. By an extra supply pipe they were kept alight all day, but the quantity of gas consumed was extremely minute. It was the duty of the Highway Committee to see that the lamps i were lighted.—Minutes confirmed. , HEALTH OF THE Tower.—The Medical Officer of Health I reported to the Health Committee that during December there were 103 births and 44 deaths, being a birth rate of .745 per 1,000, and a death rate of 1594 per 1,000. RUNCORN SAVINGS' BANK.

The annual meeting of the trustees and managers of this Bank was held yesterday afternoon, when there were present —the Revs. W. Preston and E. Williams; Messrs. .1. Brun- drit, J.P J. Simpson, J. 0. Jackson, W. Jones and W. F. Salkeld (actuary). In the absence of the Rev. Canon Bar- clay, Mr. Brundrit, with many expressions of sympathy for the absent chairman in his illness, was elected to preside. ; The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed, and the Actuary read the report for the year ended the 20. h Nov. last. Although trade had been generally depressed, the deposits had increased from £23,847 As 9d. in 1883, to £23,877 Ifs 10 last year. The assets were as follow :—With Commissioners of National Debt, £23,725 Os 101; with the treasurer to meet calls, £lB9 is 24 ; total £23,924 23; due te depositors £23,877 ifs 104, leaving a surplus of £465s 2d. He produced'the certificate of the auditors (Messrs. J. B. Salkeld, W. Brookes, Marwood, and Walter Jones) as to the correctness of the accounts —On the motion of Mr. J. 0. Jackson, seconded by the Rev. E. Williams. the repot was adopted —The Chairman proposed that a cordial vote of thanks be accorded to Mr. John Simpson, the treasurer, re- ferring in terms of eulogy to his high moral character and the admirable business capabilities he devoted to the servi- ces of the Bank. There was a great debt of gratitude owing to Mr. Simpson, not only by the trustees and managers but by the depositors, who the report showed were still increas- ing. lie hoped Mr. Simpson would be spared for many years to occupy the position of treasurer.—The Rev. W. Preston seconded the proposition, paying a tribute to Mr. Simpson's noble and upright character—The motion was carried unanimously.—Mr. Simpson, in reply, said it was 30 years since he was appointed treasurer, although he had acted as one of the managers for several year, previous to that. Mr. Salkeld was appointed secretary , at the same time, and they had got on very comfortably and very satisfactorily. (Hear, hear.) The bank had gradually progressed. The amount lodged with the National Debt Commissioners was, he thought, about three times as much now as it was 30 years ago. Of course, they could not ex- pect the increase as it was before the Pat./Moe Sayings' Bank was established, but still everything was very satis- factory. He was very sorry, indeed that Canon Barclay could not be present with them that day. He had been looking at the minute book and had discovered that the Vicar took the chair at the annual meeting in 1817, that was 35 years ago, and with one exception he had been pre- sent every year. The interest he had taken in the Savings Bank as well as in every good work in the town, must have been very gratifying to his parishioners. He (Mr. Simpson) had great pleasure in proposing that a vote of sympathy be forwarded to the Vicar.—The Rev. E. Williams seconded the motion. lie had known Canon Barclay for many years and esteemed him very highly both as a gentleman and as vicar of the parish.—The motion was carried unanimously.—On the proposition of the Rev. E. Williams, seconded by Mr. 3.0. Jackson, the auditors were thanked for their services. Mr. Simpson then movid a vote of thanks to the actuary to whose abilities and character he referred in very cordial terms. The Rev. Preston seconded, expressing the hope that Mr. Salkeld might long be spared to hold the position he had filled so satisfactorily to all concerned for so long a period. The motion was carried with applause.—ln reply Mr. Salkeld acknowledged the kind remarks made with reference to him, and said he had endeavoured to do his duty. The in- stitution was doing a great deal of good work in the town, and he hoped it would continue te prosper. lie referred to the confidence the working classes had in the bank, and said that money was occasionally repaid without the requisite notice being given. The public, particularly the working classes, the young women and servatat girls, seemed to take great pleasure in going to that tank, and be trusted this confidence would be maintained, and that Success and pros- perity would attend the institution in the future as in the past. lie announced that in consequence of the death of Mr. Thomas Johnson, formerly the treasurer of the bank who was one of his sureties, he should be required to find Another surety In Ilia stead, and he begged to propose his

Up to April 1, .1883; 139,452 railway employes were examined in Germany with reference to colour blind- ness. It was found that of these 998 had no idea of colour. Of 115,151 engaged in the general work of the service it was ascertained that 46 were completely and 273 partially inseneible to differences of colour. Among 13,616 engineers one only was completely, but 27 others i partially, n the same case. According to a telegram received at Berlin from Zan- zibar, the two brothees, Clemens and Gustav Denhardt, have arrived there to make preparations for another tour of exploration in East Africa. In the years 1878 and 1879 these German travellers explored the region between six devees and two degrees south latitude, be- tween Zanzibar and Lamu, and their present expedition seems to be organised on a comprehensive scale and. supported by several scientific societies. A New COMET.—For some time past astronomers have been expecting a comet (which completes its revolution round the sun in about three and a third years) to be- come visible. Intelligence has just been received an- nouncing that M. Tempel, of Florence, succeeded in find- ing the comet on the 13th ult. It is the first on the list of comets .of short period. It was first discovered on January, 17th, 1786, by leleehein at Paris, the periodi- city being discovered by Professor Encke about 1819. A very important work is in course of execution at Antwerp - for the illumination of dwelling-houses by the electric light, the electric current for the purpose to be distributed from a central station. The first installa- tion will be for more than 6,000 incandescent lamps; the dynamos will be on the Guleher system, and the cur- rent will be transmitted by means of -subterranean cables on the Callender system, protected with a metal casing filled with isolating material. Tins installation should be completed next February. AN iLLUMINATED TRAIN.—The use of powerful electric are lights upon .the engines of railway trains as head- lights is more common in America than in Great Britain, and it is now proposed there to utilise these lamps in another way—namely, as back-lights, illuminating the train behind, and so arranged that a beam can be shed along the side of the train at which passengers alight on arriving at a station. This improvement, if successfully carried out, will tend to prevent passengers missing their foothold in stepping out at night. Tag HELIOGRAPH IN Menavries.—An optical telegraph between the islands of Mauritius and Reunion, in the Indian Ocean, is in a fair way of being established per- manently. Heliographic signals will be exchanged between the Pie Vert mountain in Reunion and the Pouee mountain in :41auritius, so well known to readers of St, Pierre's "Paul and Virginia." Local telegraphs will carry the messages to Lacroix in the former island, and Port Louis in the latter. The communication is ex- pected to be very useful to the trade and comfort of the islands, by announcing cyclones on their way, and it was found that a submarine telegraph would cost too much to be adopted at present. How INsaers Baeleriez.—lf we take any moderately large insect, say a wasp or a hornet, we can see, even with the naked eye, that a series of small spot-like marks runs along either side of the body. These ap- parent spots, which are generally eighteen pr twenty in number, are in fact the apertures through which air is admitted into the system,, and are generally formed in such a manner that no extraneous matter can by any possibility find entrance. Sometimes they are furnished with a pair of horny lips, which can be opened and closed at the will of the insect; in other cases they are densely fringed with stiff, interlacing bristles, forming a filter, which allows air, and air alone, to pass. But the apparatus, of whatever character it may be, is always so wonderfully perfect in its action that it has been found impossible to inject the body of a dead insect with even so Subtle a medium as spirits of wine, al- though the subject was first immersed in the fluid, and then placed beneath the receiver of an air-pump.—Good Words. MORE LIGHT AND PCfRER AlR.—From a social point of view, it is almost impossible to over-estimate the nuis- ance that arises from the failure of science to solve the problem of complete combustion. Habit has accus- tomed the inhabitants of our large manufacturing cities to an amount of dirt and inconvenience which materially interferes with the common amenities of existence. The elements which all mankind—and, in fact, the whole animal kingdom—ought to enjoy as their birthright are denied to the wealthiest inhabitants of a manufacturing town. The light is obscured and the atmosphere polluted to an extent that accounts for many of the worst features of our social life. Among the labouring classes a winter spent in a large indus- trial centre is often a more trying ordeal, in all its essential elements, than banishment to the wildest and the most inhospitable regions of :nature. Rising in darkness that is frequently rendered more obscure by smoke and exhalations, they return at night to breathe the same perpetual foulness. The conditions which produce lassitude among the educated and the wealthy, rendering change of air a necessity, cannot be supposed to leave those who are more constantly sub- jected to their influence unaffected by their continual presence. It seems unreasonable to expect that the prescriptions of the physician for the better classes, in the form of tonics, should not find their counterpart among the working classes in the shape of stimulants, with all their concomitant evils of drunkenness and crime. One may safely say that the moral effects of this failure of science to solve the problem of complete combustion are to be estimated as a great national calamity. The physical results are even more apparent. The labour necessary to combat with the dirt arising from the smoke of a great city must of itself be equal to any one of its largest industries. Unfortunately, this labour falls to the share of those who are already over- burdened. It too often overpowers the exertions of the workman's wife, who at last gives up the contest, and contents herself with the constant contact of squalor. Let any one estimate for himself the money value repre- sented by the labour necessary to clean the windows, and sweep the chimneys, and beat the carpets, and wash the extra linen of such a city as Manchester, and he will then discover the social importance of complete combus- tion.—Great Industries of Great Britain. UNDERGROUND HAULAGE BY ELECTRICITY IN A GER- MAN COLLIERY.—At a recent meeting of the Mining In- , stitute of Scotland, a paper was read by Mr. Robert Thomas Moore, C.E. B.Sc., entitled "Notes on some Saxon Collieries." bile of the mines visited by the author during the past autumn was the Zaukeroda Colliery at Piauen near Dresden, which belongs to the Government. A; a special feature of the appliances in use at this colliery, the author remarked that there is one of Siemens and Halske's electrical locomotives drawing coals along one of the underground roadways over a distance of 700 yards-. Driven by belting from a small vertical engine having its cylinder inverted and with its pulleys about three to one, there is on the surface the primary dynamo machinery, which is run at about 600 revolutions per minute, while the engine has a speed of about 200 revolutions per minute. The current from the dynamo is carried down the pit shaft, which is about 120 fathoms deep, by means of quarter-inch copper rods, and along the level roadway it is conveyed by means of two rails of T-section which are fastened .to the roof of the mine. The road, which is a cross- cut mine for getting over a fault, is laid with a double line of rails, and is arched with bride throughout its whole extent. Porcelain insulators are fixed in the brickwork for carrying the con- ductors. There is a secondary dynamo on the loco- motive, which is connected to the wheels of the latter by means of gearing. Each pole of the dynamo commu- nicates with one of the conductors on the roof by means of a covered wire, one end of which is fastened to a car- riage running on the rail, and the other to a pole of the dynamo. The "race" consisted of 15 tubs, each contain- ing.lo cwt., and when loaded 15 cwt. The locomotive was put behind the "race" and ran the whole length of the drift in four minutes, or at about the rate of seven miles an hour. It was making 25 runs per day, and drawing about 200 tons in that period. Mr. Moore learned that the following was the proportion of useful. effect of the arrangement :—Steam engine, ten-horse power, and the dynamo and locomotive, respectively five and three horse power, from which it was concluded that 30 percent. of the power of the steam engine Was got out of the locomotive. The cost of the whole erec- tion at the colliery was about £9OO, and the system has been in operation for nearly two years, the engine working very satisfactorily, giving no trouble, and the working expenses being very low. As the cost of repairs was almost nil, the chief expenses consisted of the wages of the enginemen on the surface and on the locomotive.— Engineering. -

Now I beg most respectfully as a towhee, but rust -emphatically as a ratepayer, to pro- test against the coompuisued by the Educational authority of Runcorn. _ _ .

Firstly: Because whenever the idea—" It is not a bit of use this B hard sitting unless it dose-something "—fleshes into its mind, it resorts to great economy of truth in order to find something tulle- In support of this, I unequivocally deny, that the child Wright was ever refused admission at this school. The facts ale simply these : He was admitted here about June last (although in attainments only fit for an infant school) upon the terms named to all children applying for admission, vie., that so leng as he attended regularly the fee would b 3,3 I for standard 1, paid weekly in advance; if he should attend irregularly 6,1 per week would be demanded' This is a reeolutien passed at a duly con- vened managers' riveting, for the purpose of co-operating with the Board iu securing regularity, and has had a bene- ficial effect upon many la.ls whose attendance was previ- ously careless. During the first month that Wright was a scholar he was absent eight times only, but du.inz the next two months he made 44 out of a possible 76 attendances. Messages and notes were sent to his mother reminding her of the conditions under which the crud was entered, but all were alike unavailing, and the higher fee was imposed and paid for three weeks, with a better attend- ance. For week ended 21 November 31 was again accepted as fees, and irregularity recommenced the child being ab- 'sent four times during the week and the whole of the 811C0 needing one. About Wednesday, 26 November, I sent a warning respecing fee., and received in reply from his mother the message, "He has left Your school!' A week later, e.g., after a week and two days; absenc, Mrs. Wright appeared at school seeking re-admission for her child; I reminded her of her message, adding, " His name had been struck off our books," when she said, have tried to get him into the other schools, but they will not have him." My answer was," Well, his fee is fid per week," to which she replied, "I shall not pry 6d. I will keep him at home first," and took the lad off the premises. That the mane- I gers are strictly within their rights is proved by the ruling of that tribunal to which the clerk to the Board is so anxious I to appeal, and forwarded by it to the Huddersfield Board in a case somewhat analogous to this. For the edification of your readers, sir, and the instruction of the clerk, it is not the first official instruction I have furnished him with—l give it verbatim et literatim:— Education Dst aqment, 15 Feb nary, 1.831.—1 am to paint I out that so long as the fee does nit exceed 91 per week it rests w th the minagera of vo:untary s-tho is 0 decide whit fee they shall thirge in any pasticalar case. tam further to state that my lords are of opinion iii at the rnanag,ers of a schoal are justified In charging a hig'aer fee in the case of children capriciously withheld froin the annual inspection or are cariclously removed from school. —(4lgued) J XILLHB. Th it Wright was not a regular scholar, as assated by a charitable member may be gathered from the fact that he made 101 out of a p ossiele 130 attendances during the time his name was on our ooks ; and that he was capriciously rentoved c innot be disputed. Farther, I gather that I am charged with imposing in- creased fees upon all boat children after absence—this is a gross inaccuracy. There are in school at the present time 36 children whose parents obtain a livelihood by working the river and canal traffic; of these 3 only pay increased

fees, whilst 5, other than 1-oat children are also charged the higher rate. Once more, the Clerk is reported to have said that representations on the matter of Wright had been made to the Schoolmasters on several occasions. I deny this in tote, the attendance officer called once upon me in reference to the case, when I distinctly told him that no boy was ever rofustd admission by me providing h 3 had his fee. I protest secondly (as a ratepayer) against a paid officer of the Board having all the talk and almost going to the length of making•propositions ; it is high time the Board I had the moral courage to teach this official his place and duty, for, sir, invariably the reports of the Board's meetings consists simply of the Clerk's eloquence. Thirdly, against the high-handed and autocratic beariag of the Board—advised by the Clerk. For before deciding upon th 3 rash act of appealing to the Education Department (no practical man would have dreamt of such a coarse) would it not hive bedn an act of courtesy to have adopted the Chairman's suggestion ant have written to the schools— not to the Masters, of course not, bat to the Managers ask- ing if so-and-so were true? The Board would then have had chapter and verse for any representation it may have seen fit, in its wisdom, to transmit to the central authority. Evidently not only teachers but the majority, at least' of managers in Runcorn are too plebeian for tLe clerk to held correspondence with. I beg to conclude, sir, by asking Mr. Norman two ques- tions. _ _

_ 1. Whether it is not a fact that at the school of which he is a manager children in standard IV. and upwards are charged 61 per week, and have to find in addition a reading book, ranging from 2s to 3a. Here the fees are 41. and books provided by managers. • 2. Why doesn't he look after those over whom be has a little jurisdiction, and sea that they keep the law ? _He would then assist in saving the School Board the loss of a c vie, and the ratepayers the cost arising out of the said case; vide police news of Monday last. The public attack on me is my apology for this lengthy letter, but I beg to request that as you published the charge in extenso, you will at least bestow upon me the same favour.—Yours faith- fully, T. H. ANNETE.

TEETOTALISM AT EARLESTOWN. Sir,—After carefully reading on th peered in your valued pin theenbletovtoeros wubihoolcthlhoaovme come to the conclusion that a mere word controversy is being waged, with what good result I know not. First of all "a Disgusted Teetotaller" hears a statement from a Wesleyan pulpit which does not snit his p aticular fancy. He retires from the Chapel and henceforth vows vengeance- on " Moderation" and the preacher alike. The minister referred to is known to him and one would think that in an common sense the most straightforward and gentlemanly course would be to appeal to the "certain Rev, gentleman" who made the statement to supply proof. lint no, " Disgusted Teetotaller" rushes into print with an angry, curt note, and under the I oloak of asking the public to answer the statement, thrusts a venomous dart at the minister in the name of teetotalism. Now I dare venture to assert that if the certain Bev. gentle. man had been properly appealed to he would have been both willing arid competent to have produced biblical prof, and there the subject might have ended. But it seems this would not have suited "Disgusted Teetotaller." He must needs write a letter, which, although brief, contained suffi- cient force to drive away a multitude of would be support- ers, yet not enou,h kindness and charity that would draw a single convert. It is by such conduct that teetotalism fails to make more progrets—people become "disgusted" with the subject through the indiscretion and rash acts of its so-called champions. Whatever we may say of "Moder- ation," oh that we had more of it exhibited, not as regards eating and drinking only, but all round—in our tempers and outward conduct towards our brethren, even though they may happen to differ from us. As regards the case in dispute, the rev, gentleman was re. questel to deal with the subject on Temperance Sunday by those who knew his views perfectly well, and then when he had publicly stated them they took offence and (says one correspondent) some vow they will never go to hear him again. And all this bee ins° he applied " temperance" all round, rather than in its one respect as regards drink. What is the conclusion outsiders will draw ? That teeto- talism is being substituted for raigion (which embraces all the virtues) and that all those who dare to speak differently must be scouted and forsaken, be they ministers or laymen. From such miserable narrow-mindedness may we all be delivered. There is too much work In the world for Chris- tians to do to justify them quibbling on words, and the sooner "Disgusted Teetotaller" and his friends realizs this and unite in a friendly spirit in attempting to put down evil of all kinds, the sooner will success be evident —Yours truly, • CONSTANT READER. RArlestowo, January 12th, 1685.

div.head: TOWN COUNCIL AND THE MEASLES.
div.p: THE TOWN COUNCIL AND THE MEASLES.

see that the Council has been haying a " big " debate about the measles, and have come to the conclusioa to try more rigid methods to stamp the disease out from among children. This seems on the first blush a very laud- able conclusion to come to, but does it not go to show how contradictory are the ways of would-be protectors bf the public health? Oise of their ways of coping with disease is to haul children by c,)mpullion to a public vaccinator to be inlculated with a mediae.] form of small-pox, while now it is proposed to haul by compulsiou the same children to a public hospital to be out of the way of measles, I ask where is the consistency of two such seemingly contradic- tory modes of dealing with disease? Upon what principle are they based? Vaccination is defended on the theory that by infecting children with a modified form of small- , pox the substance upon which the germs of the more deadly ' forms of the dims(' feed is removed from the body. and the disease thus prevented from gaining a foothold. Now, ac-

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURD kY, JANUAR
div.p: EXAMINER. SATURD kY, JANUAR

" -.--, I cording to this theory, if children were not vaccinated but were protected from small-pox by the cases which did break , out amongst them being carefully isolated the result would clearly he that those who had not been touched by the disease would grow up with the substance in their body upon which the germs are nourished, and they would con- l sequently be continually liable to be struck down. The I child would be protected at the expense of the man and the woman who had perhaps in the meantime become the breadwinner or the mother of a family. That would clearly prove to be a cruel sort of kindness. I believe that all medern re- search goes to show that smallpox and measles, and other contagious diseases are very much alike in the nature of their origin aed propagation, and therefore the reasoning which applies to one appiLs to the other. It would be a strange result of the paternal solicitude of Alelerman Bur- gess and his committee if it were found that measles were brcoming less frequent amongst children and more frequent amongst grown-up people. Who knows but that the pre- sent remarkable immunity from the disease amongst adults, is due to the fact that almost every child has it. The idea that every child is fated to have the measles some thne or other is well knawn to be prevalent amongst what are known as the lower classes. This is of course branded as a vulgar superstition by the perhaps over-sapient sanitarians , who figure on Town Councils and Local Boards, bet after all it is not so much a superstition as an unconscious induc- tion from a wide range of experience and observation. It may be that in this instance, as in some other, the general sense of the masses may be more in the right than some of the " faculty " who, like Dr. Slegrado,alweys have some pet theory about bleeding or "aqueous draughts," or some, thing else. At any rate one could feel better pleased with the intentions of the Council if one could be sure that they were not going to some extent to violate the very principle upon which vaccination itself is based. INQUIRER.

div.head: TRADE DEPRESSION.
div.p: TRADE DEPRESSION.

Sir,—Your correspondent, "Fair Protit," "whoever he may be," seems to suggest a went of consistency on my part. Well, I have not much respect for that same trouble- some jade, and am quite prepared, at any time, to throw her overboard. There is an old saying, "Teat wise men change their minds; fools never do." Having said this much, I must confess that in this case I do not see where the want of consistency comes in. Instead of "Fair Profit ' trying to be "smart," he ouetst to have drawn my attention to the couflicting statements referred to. All the same, I must acknowledge the fair spirit la which his letter is written, and hope that, with a lit is more experience, his view of things, social and political, will eventually become as broad as my own. When one writes to the public press, or speaks on the public platform, it should be with the view of imparting information. This has not been my primary object, but rather to prove to my fellow workmen that there is a vehicle ready made to their hands by which they may con- vey to the public, and spread anion:set each other their thoughts, and their grievances. It may be that writers like "Fair Profit" will charge them with writing " foolishly." Never mind this. Neither lack of grammar, nor yet that abundance of sense so conspicuous in our Fair Trade opponents, should deter us from making use of the press, se long as the rules of decency are wisely superin- tended by a discriminating editor. I should scarcely feel flattered were any one to charge me with being a" leveller." An old awl obsolete word this, Mr. Editor. Very likely "Fair Profit" Dever heart of it, or he would have attached it to my fair fame, and thereby have sullied it. Equality in possessions is no Bearer attainment than equality in brains. It were foolishnees to strive for it, yet I may point this fact out, that the best brains of to-day are striving earnestly for a means of bridging over the ever- widening and increasingly dangereus gulf that now separates labour from capital. I must tell " Fair Profit "that I envy no man his possessions, under the present social conditions. It is only foil >wing out the inevitable law of cause and effect. Alter the cause and the effect will disappear. Stop S r Gilbert Greenall from brewing ale, and the appearance of the streets of Warrington will morally change as if by magic. (Ibeg Fair Profit" will not mention the word consistency.) The firms referred to " lived in prosperous times, when the introduction of machinery made more fortunes than ever were made before." Will "Fair PI Ofit " give us his opinion how far this same signature of his entered into the engage- ment between workman arid employer, so that the workman might receive all that was in excess of fair profit? If your correspondent will refer to the 'Fortnightly " for November, he will there find an article, " Tne future of Industry," the views in which I completely endorse. I think it is a mis- take to say, generally speaking, that our manufacturers are itivestiog their earnings in foreign securities. I hive noticed various charges of this sort recently, and the emphatic con- tradictions given have bean sufficiently convincing. Capital at home is b log organized with a completeness pre- viously unknown, with which the hitherto followed plan of trade unionists will ba unable to cope. What is plain at present is, that all our advances in machinery bring no lei- sure to the workman, unless it be after the fashion of America, where I see it stated that the manufacturers can produce as much in six months as can be consumed in twelve —which really means six months distress to the workman. Respecting the charge of foolishness, I must say it is somewhat hasty. Increased number of works means in- creased production; increased home compethion and in- creased attraction to those who ought to remain England's proud peasantry. Has "Fair Profit" ever thought it out how much useless work is done in this Eiglantl of ours? I pro- mise him a few more of my ideas on this subject at an early date. In the meantime he can think upon it. I am thank- ful that I have managed to write one "sensible sentence;" but my critic seems to hoof opinion that the present Govern- ment alone of all previous Governments is to blame for neglecting to put things right at home. Let us see; soup kitchens in Warrington have not, I think, been known since this Government came in. Perhaps my critic may rernems ber the date of their introduction to the notice of our work- ing poor. Neither have town councillors felt called upon to suggest a surgical operation in support of elathu- sianism. He may also remember th's freak of a local Tory. In 1879 a public speaker stated" wages are lower than they have been at any time during the last twenty years." In the Cleveland iron district shops were closed because people had not money to purchase the necessaries of life. More than one third of tha houses erected for miners were then standing empty. In Lancashire the whole of the cotton trade was suffering Ist similar fashion, and claims were made for the reduction of wages on every side. The Times of February 23th, 1879, stated that the distress in Sheffield was so terrible that the means for relieving it were nearly exhausted, and a wail was made for general assistance. In Cornwall the distress was snore severe than had been known for the last fifty years. In Kent, Surrey, Sasses, Norfolk, Wiltshire, and Dorsetshire a fearful cry came from the agri- cultural ',thou-ere, and when Sir Stafford Northcete referred to the distress in the House of Commons, he was met by a laugh from his own supporters. Mr. J. Maden Holt, one of the members for North-east Lancashire, a Tory, said," there were cycles of prosperity, and the poor Tories had always tumbled into cycles of distress." Sir Edmund Beckett, a Tory, and the greatest opponent to trades unionism England has in it, stated trade had been driven away to America on account of the Willenhall lock makers claiming too high wages. We all rernambar how this was disproved. Does "pair Profit" went a little more of the history of England's 'trade during the last adminis- tration? If so, let him Coma nearer hems and remember what happened to the trade he seems t) have taken under his special care; during the wise and patriarchial govern- ment of him whom Bishop Wilberforce. then a guest of Lord Salisbury, termed "the tricky Disraeli." I refer to the im- mense reduction in the wiredrawers' wage list. all these things happened during the reign of the Tories; yet there was no cry for Protection. What a grievous thing that corn "should ba at a lower price than ever it was known before," and yet only make one halfpenny per loaf difference to the purchaser. Our Fair Traderes all wrong on this question as usual. If he will prevail upon corner-men, middle-men, and bakers to be satisfied with " fair profits," the producer and the consumers would have a better chance. While all other trades are " barely getting change for a shilling," the bakers throughout the kingdom are making fertunes. The combination amongst master bakers is of such an injurious chiracter that the public press did good service recently in exposing it. I am rather at a loss to know how "mere theorists and newspaper men " benefit by the British working-men losing ten shillings a week through reduction in his wages and loss of time. Please explain. I have more than , once put a simple question to Fair Traders, yet I can get no answer. Will they kindly select one trade as an examisle and show how the country would benefit by haying it protected ? So that there may be no wandering from the subject, I chal- lenge the Protectionists to make good their position upon this One point, and I suggest the wire trade for the exposi- tion of their principles. I can fancy nothing' so useful as a guide for legislation or social questions as the experience gained in the past. I have before net nose tlse " Quarterly Review " for 1842, in which there is an article on Colliers and Collieries. It is simply heartrending to read it, men and women, lads and lasses, working in the pits together. Mary Barrett, aged 14 : "I always works without stockings, shoes, or trowsers. I wear nothing but a shift • I have to go up the headings with tlao men. They are all netted there." " Females sub- mit to work in ;41aces where no man could be got to labour. In a posture nearly double, they are below till the last hour of pregnancy." I give these as samples of the pesition of workmen during the era of protection, and I have just at my elbow graphic descriptions as to the unenviable position of the ribbon weavers of Coventry, the stockingers and lace workers of Nottingham. Let those working-men who are slightly disposed to favour this wild notion of Fair Trade Bit down and think over the matters calmly, try to fathom what it means, and compare the present with the past. If Protection is a remedy for bad trade, the distressed indus- tries of this country ought to be prosperous in Protectionist countries, but, as a matter of fact, they are worse off, alike in Germany, France, and America. There are workmen who think their own especial trade ought to ba protected. If we have it at all, in common justice we must go all rouhd. Now, as a matter of fact, our imports of manufactured goods are not much more than one-tenth of our total im- ports. " Fair Prs.fit " may talk of Henry George's " revo- lutionary doctrines." Why not protest against the acts and doings of Mr. Winans, the American millionaire? But at this point I beg to be excused from going into the land question; not only this, but the recent doings of the rail- way companies call for most stringent inquiries, and could so•called well-wishers of the British workman see their was clear to united action, the voting power now within their reach would to a certainty be fraught with naught but good for all concerned. CLIFFORD DIX.

div.head: Y 17, 1885
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

On Monday a severe snowstorm prevailed in various parts the c)untiv, and the cold was intense. Of the £50,000 required for church extension in cennec- tion with the Bishop of Newcastle's fund, £40,000 has al- ready been promised. The political jubilee of the Right Hon. C. P. Villiers, who has represented Wolverhampton in Parliament for fifty years, was celebrated on Saturday. Numerously-signed petitions continue to be forwarded to the Home Secretary for the release of Dudley and Stephens, recently convicted in the Mignonette case. The Catholic Bishop of Elphin has dissolved a new and flourishing Catholic temperance s,ciety in Sligo, called the Green Ribbon Society. It is said that a secret society might spring from it. The Mayor and Mayoress of Liverpool on Monday even- ing entertained about 400 juvenile guests at a fancy-dress ball at the Town Hall. and subsequently about 900 adults were present at a full-dress assembly. The Oswestry Rural Board have refused to allow the words" Of your charity pray for the soul" (of the departed) to be placed on a stone erected over the remains of a former inhabitant of the town, who was a Roman Catholic. The manager of a large condensed milk factory at Mid- dlewich has notified to the Cheshire dairy farmers that in future he will receive no milk obtained frem cows fed upon ensilage, as such milk is altogether unfitted for condens- ing.

ARREST OF A SUPPOSED TRIPLE MURDERER.—WiIIiam Sheehan, who is suepected of having committed a tripla murder at Castletown Ache, Cork, where three bodies were found in a well, has been arrated in New Zealand by the colonial police. The Admiralty on Saturday invited tenders from Belfest shipbuilding firms for the building of six cruisers similar to those now being built by Messrs. Thompson, of Belmuir. The cruisers will be of the Scout type, and the contracts were decided upon almost immediately. THE FATAL QUARRY ACCIDENT.—The Coroner for Car- narvoeshire, on Tuesday, resumed an inquiry into the death of six men killed by the fall of earth at the Dorothea Quarries, on the 29th ult. The fatality was attributed to the percolation of water from a lak 3 in the locality, and the jury returned a verdict of " Aceidental death." INHUMANITY AT SEA.—The trial of Renscher and Koel- pen for the murder of the seaman Jansen on the American ship J. F. Ch apm in was concluded at Bow-street, London, on Tuesday. Further evidence was given by the crew of the habitual ill-tresement of J moon by the prisoners. Sir James Ingham expressed his intention of sending them to take their trial in America. AN OLD WOMAN.—A. well-known Welsh spinster, Mar- garet Morris, residing in the perish of Llancynfelin, near lAberystwith, hee just attained the remarkable age of 107 years. The fact is authenticated by the list of paupers in which her name, with her age appended, has been enrolled for many years. She is comparatively hale, and is able to move about, but her memory and sight have almost wholly failed her. THE L aTE LORD LYTTON'S LOVE LETTERS—JO the Chancery Division, on Monday, Mr. .Aiethold moved, in the action of Lord Lytton v. Miss Davy, who is the sole executrix of the late Lady Lytton, mother of the plain- tiff, by consent of all parties, for an order making perpetual the injunction restraining the defendant from publishing the letters of the late Lord Lytton to his wife. The de- fendant agreed to pay the costs of the action, and the order was made.

SPE,Ca BY MR BRADLAUGII.—.• Mr. Bradlaugh speaking at Ketting Corn Exchange on Monlay night, denounced the feeling displayed in this country regtrdiug Germany, and attributed the depression in trade, both here and throughout Europe, to the en•rmous war establishments which are kept up and the military promenades which are indulged in. He was glad to see that a new member of the Government (Mr. Cain) had pronounced in favour of one House of Parliament. _

STURSIIAW CROSS V. BRYN GATE BLUES.—Played On the ground of the former on Saturday, and after an exciting game victory rested with the Jaime team by one goal to nil. NEWTON V. Cuorrant. This match should have been played at Newton on Saturday, but the visitors sent word durin the week that they could not raise a team and the match must be cincelled.

NICHOL-LANE V. EARLESTOWN RAMBLERS (2ND TEAMS). —Played on Saturday at Earlestown and resulted in a dis- pute, the Ramblers having scored two goals and Nichol- lane three goals and one disputed. Sr. PETER'S SCHOOLS BRYN, V. BIRCHLEY SCHOOLS, BILLINOE.—PIayed at Billinge on Saturday. St. Peters were the victors by two goals to nil. The sec md teams met at Bryn, and St. Peters won by five goals to nil. ASHTON RECREATION V. HINDLEY GREEN. (IRO. Played at Ifindley Green on Saturday, and ended in a vic- tory for the visitors by four goals to three. The second teams met at Ashton. and the match ended in a victory for the borne team by two goals to nil. OUGIITRINGTON V. WIDNES (A. TEAM). The Widnes team turned up at Heatley, on Saturday, with a very good team, while the home players were without the service of Jackson, Lord, Davies, and Gosling. After an hour's good play tba game ended in a draw, the score being two minor points for the home team, to Widnes four minor points. WARRINGTON V. BCRY.—Played On the ground of the ' former on Saturday, when there were about 400 spectators present. The toss was won by the Bury c iptein who elec- ted to play with the wind. The game was an exciting one, and at the call of time the score Cood—Warrington, one goal, five tries, and seven minors to nil. The back play of Walsh was very fine, Barnes. Massey, and Gilbert also play- ing in good form. Those of the front most prominent were Jolley, Robinson, Rigby, and Turner, Hargreaves played a good back game. The pick of the others were Howarth and Ormerod, and forward \rose, J. Nuttall, and Entwistle. Teams :—Warrington : Back, T. Walsh ; three-quarters, J. T. Massey, T. Barnes, and T. Balshaw ; half-backs, W. Speakman and E Gilbert ; forwards, H. Ashton (cmtain), F. Turner, W. Povey, J. Robiasoo, J. Rigby, W. Dillon, J. Jolley, and Tony Davies. Bary : Back, Hargreaves; three-quarters, Porter, Howarth, and Senior ; half-backs, Ormerod and Fletcher ; forwards,. J. Nuttall (captain), Vose Smith, Entwistle, Ogden, Frank Turner, F. Nuttall, Buxtoa, Sankey. EARLESTOWN V. HAYDOCK Sr. JAMES'S. Played at .EArlestown on Saturday for the benefit of a former player in the St. James's team, who had his leg broken some months age. There was a large attendance considering the incle- ment state of the weather. The visitors were but poorly represented, five second team men appearing in their ranks. Up to half-time the St. James's men pressed their opponents, and on a few occasions nearly scored. The defence of the Earlestown backs and half-backs was too good, though on one occasion the leather was put through the Eirles-own . . .

goal, but the point was disallowed on a claim of " off-side." On the change of ends the Earlestonians had matters nearly all their own way, and the home team were forced to act on the defensive. When time, was called Earlestown retired the victors by one goal (scored by Harrison) to none. Teams : Earlestown : J. Appleton, goal ; R. Green and J. Green, backs; R. Bowker, J. Duxbury, and A. Clayton, half-backs ; H. Holcroft and J. Wil HAMS, light wing ; W. Murray, centre ; W. Rich and J. Harrison, left wing ; umpire, J. Sim'. St. James's : J. King, goal ; R. Rmmer and H H. Anderton backs; T. King, A. Ander- ton, and T. Pirnblett, half-backs ; W. Williams and T. Moran, right wing; H. Mayhew and M. Arnold. left wing; referee, Mr. Pomfret. EARLESTOWN WANDERERS V. STANLEY.-118 Wanderers' Committee write as follows:—"In connection with the above club in regard to the Liverpool and District Cup competition the Wanderers' Committee consider that they have been unjustly dealt with. In the first match the Wanderers beat their opponents honestly by three goals to two. Not one of the spectators left the ground with the idea that a protest would be lodged against the home team on the ground that the game was an unfair one. The cap- tain of the home team requested the opinion of the Stanley players after they left the ground, and their answer was that they were satisfied with everything but the result. Notwith- standing this declaration a protest was lodged, and on the following Monday a telegram was received by the secretary of the home team, requesting the umpire to appear before the Association Committee in Liverpool. The re- sult wag, after the statement of the referee and the two umpires that it was a fair game, that the match must be played over'again. This was a violation of the spirit cf rule 16, which states distinctly that the two competing clubs shall give intimation of all protests at the time the violation takes place, or before they leave the ground. No such in- timation was given. After the protest was lodged and car- ried against the home team, public feeling became excited against Stanley, and the result was, on the occasion of the second aupeiranee of the visitors, the collection of youths of the village, who gave them a very unwelcome reception, much against the wishes of the committee of the Wanderers' Club and players, who condemned the proceedings, but were powerless to prevent them. After the second match, which ended in another defeat for Stanley, a lengthy report was published justly condemning the reception given to the visitors. After seeing the report they decided to clear them- selves from all blame." NOTES BY THE WAY. . _

A PAMPER'S WINDFALL.—An elderly man named Jennes, has just come in for a fortune, in the shape of property in Yorkshire, which is said to be worth two million pounds: Jennes formerly worked for Mr. Titmarsh, ironmonger, Sur- rey, but getting bee ond work has since depended on parish relief, and such assistance as his friends in the neighbour- hood could give him. He has been counting on his fortune for years past, hut it has only just come to him. The affair has made quite a sensation in the neighbourhood. ExECuTlON.—Horace Jay was executed at Wandsworte Gaol on Tuesday, for the murder of his sweetheert, Florence Kemp. The prisoner stabbed her at his lodgings, Clapham, while in a it of jealousy. He paid great attention to the chaplain's ministrations, but maintained throughout that the murder was for the girl's good, because saving her from a world of trouble. He slept soundly on Monday night, and walked with a firm step to the eceffold. Berry was the executioner, and gave a drop of 7ft. Death appeared to be instantaneous. Ica ACCIDENTS —Two boys were drowned at Farnworth on Wednesday by the giving way of the ice on a "lodge" of water which they had ventured to cross. A peculiarly painful accident also occurred on Wednesday at Wrexham, where a number ef boys were immersed in a pond through the breaking of the ice, and three brothers named Jones sons of a police sergeant, were drowned. A boy named Lyons, an inmate of the Barnes Home Industrial School at Heaton Mersey, and employed at a neighbouring works, fell through the ice upon which he was sliding, on Wednesday, and was drowned A youth of 14, named Walker, son of the vicar of Albrighton, Shrewsbury, was drowned on Thursnay, in a pool near his father's residence, on which he had been skating. Two girls, aged 16, named Wetton and Owen, Were drowned while skating at Darlaston on Thursday. PROPORTIONAL REPRESENTATION.—LETTERS FROM THE PREMIER AND LORD SALISBURY.-111r. Albert Grey, M.1'.., has received letters from the Premier and Lord Salisbury on proportional representation. Mr. Gladstone says :—" I can- not wonder at your laying stress en the support given, as I understand, to proportional representation in the strict form in which Mr. Courtney expounded it. You will not expect from me at the present stage any further declaration of the feasibility of the plan, but I am very glad that you will be the more able, from the foothold obtained in your own country, to secure its being well weighed ley the public at large, for to this full examination it is certainly entitled considering what are the claims it makes and who are the people that support it." Lord Salisbury says:—" I shall be very glad to hear an account of the counting and sorting of the ballot papers at your model election." A HOUSEKEEPER SHOT By MisTAKE.—A tragic incident occurred early on Tuesday at Lockwood. a suburb of Hud- dersfield. A widower named Thomas Walker Holmes, who has been for 14 veers employed in the Huddersfield flank, was awakened at his residence by hearing a noise down- stairs. He went down, taking a revolver with him and as he descended the first flight one chamber accidentally went off, alarming the. inmates. Holmes called out, asking who was there, and receiving no answer, fired again. On pia- needing to the kitchen he found his housekeeper, Mary Blackburn, a woman 45 years old, lying on the floor. She had been shot in the right eye, and died before assistance could be procured. Holmes was under the impression that burglars were in the house. He is greatly respected in the neighbourhood as a steady industrious man. At Hudders- field, on Wednesday, Mr. Holmes was remanded until Thursday on ball. His legal repreeentative stated that there had been no deliberate shooting at the supposed thief, but an aimless discharge of the revolver, intended merely to frighten. GOLBORNE. SUICIDE OF A BREWERY MANAGER AT HALEWOOD. On Thursday afternoon an inquest was held on the body of John Ockleshaw, 48 years of age, head manager at the brewery, Halewood, a gentleman well known in commercial Circles in Liverpool, before Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner for this division, at the Eagle and Child Inn, Hale- wood. The deceased committed suicide on Tuesday even- ing by shooting himself in the heed at his residence, Hale- Wood.—Mr. William Thomas Oekleshaw, son of the de- ceased, said that on Tuesday evening his father was in the breakfast roon, playing with the children, and shortly after witness left he heard the report of a gun. On going to make inquiries he found his father lying dead in a closet in the upper part of the house with a wound in his head and a re- cently discharged gun near him. The deceased had been in very bad health, suffering chiefly from rheumatism, while his eyesight was failing, and cussing him to be ' anxious and low spirited.—Mr. Benjamin Tighe, an excise officer, who was in the house that evening, said that he saw the deceased in the closet, the wound he had indicted in his head Nina terrible one. Deceased had been chatting with Lim a few moments before, and he seemed to be in better spirits than he had been for some time. Deceased complained of his head occasionally.—A juryman remarked I that the deceased bad said that the rheumatic pains had left his body and gone to his bead.—Other evidence of a similar nature to the foregoing iraving been given, Mr. David Alexander WKnight, of the firm of Messrs. Blease and Son, chartered accountants, Liverpool, said that the books of the deceased had been audited a few days before the occurrence, and were found in perfect order, and the business was in a prosperous condition.—A verdict of " Suicide whilst in a state of unsound mind " was re- turned.

EARLESTOWN„ 4 a ALLEGIID ASSAULT ON A MOTE= AT BITIVONWOOD.— John Heaton was summoned at the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday last for assaulting his mother, Jane Heaton, at Burton wood, on theist inst.—The -complainant did not ap- pear, and as it was stated she was too ill to appear, the case vas adjourned until the neat court day. • '• .Ho

Was Goon TIDSLPLABY. —The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Lodge-room. Bridge-street, on Monday evening, under the presidency of Brc her John Taylor, W.C.T. There was a fair attendance of members. The programme was " Expe- rience and Prayer Meetin.r.," and in its carrying out the members spent an enjoyable evening. TILE ALLEGED Ouvg&ar GI A GIRL. -- In an an`e room at the Newton Tewn Hall on Saturday, before Messrs R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and C. Pilkington, Thomas Stoke;, a lad. 15 years of age, residing in Earlestown' was brought up on remand on a charge of criminally assaulting Mary Jane Williams, a girl 10 years of age, whose parents reside at Sutton, near St. Helens. The girl was on a visit to some relations at Earlestows, and on Christmas Eve was sliding on some ice covering a pond at Earlestown. She afterwards alleged that the prisoner took her on the slide and committed the assault with which he was charged. After a lengthened h?aring, the magistrates dismissed the

case. THE Nitta LOCAL RAILWAY.—The proposed new railway from St. Helens. through Parr, Haydock, Ashton, Go!borne, and opening up a new connection with South- East Lancashire, is stila creating considerable interest in the districts likely to be effected. It is stated that in accord- ance with statutary requirements the promoters have de- posited the sum of £10,160, which is equal to 5 per cent. upon the amount of the engineer's estimate for the con- struction of the line, viz, £=209,035 10s. Full confidence in the ultimate success of the scheme is manifested, and a reqaieition to his Worship• the Mayor asking him to c ill a town's meeting in support of the bill has been numerously signed. Friday, the 9th inst., was the last day for present. jog memorials against the bill, but none were lodged, and the bill, therefore, in its preliminary stages will proceed as an unopposed measure. TEE LoNDON AND NORTII•WESTEEN RAILWAY COM- PANT AND THEIR WOntotEN.—A few weeks ago we reported the dismissal, owing to slackness of trade, of over 100 workmen employed at the Viaduct Waggon Works, Endes- town, b2longing to the London and North-Western Railway Company, while at the same time many other employes were put on short time to the extent of four days per week. , The depression is still severely felt by the company in its various branches of labour, and it is stated that unless there is are improvement before long there will be further dis- charges. Orders were issued on Monday for the discharge of 100 men from the locomotive works of the company at Crewe. A large number of the furnacemen have received notice that they will be put on short time, namely four days a week. A general reduction of the staff is being made up and down the system, and if the depression continues several thousand warkmen altogether will be stopped. ORGAN RECLTAL AT NEWTON. The fourth of a series of organ recitals to clear off the debt at present ealet- ing on the organ in the Congregational Church, Crow-lane, Newton, was given in that place of worship on Thursday by Mr. Jas. Lowe, of Manchester. Notwithstanding the bitterly cold weather, there was a large congregation. Mr. Lowe excellently rendered selections front the works of Handel, Mozart, Thayer, and other composers; and Miss Wallington, Warrington, effectually sang Come unto me" (Coenen), "Jerusalem" (Mendeissohn), and I know that my Redeemer li•-ieth" (Handel). Miss Wallington was ac- companied on the organ by Mr. Lowe. In announcing a collection in aid of the organ fund the Rev. James Atha (pastor) remarked that the next recital would be given in February by their friend Mr. Blacow, of Manchester. He wished to take that opportunity of saying in the name of the committee and himself how deeply they were indebted to the generosity of Mr. Lowe and Miss Wallington for the organ recital and the concert that had been given. A col- lection was then made. WESLEYAN MrenorasT StraznaY SatOOL.—An enter- tainment in connection with:the Juvenile branch of the Wesleyan Methodist Baud of Hope Society was held in the Brunswick Wesleyan School, Cross-lane, Earlestown, en , Thursday evening. There was a fair attendance, and Mr. ' J. H. Graham presided. The evening's programme included addresses by the Chairman and Mr. D. B. Griffiths ;recita- tion, " Break the chair," Mr. Thomas Pickett ; recitation, "The yarn of the Nancy Bell," Mr. F. Cooper; and read- ing," How an Irishwoman cured her husband," by Mr. J. H. Graham. Mr. Wm. Clare (secretary) made a statement as to the terms of membership for the coming year. A meeting of the members of the Senior Band of Hope Society was afterwards held under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Hep- wood. After the opening remarks of the Chair Man, Mr. Wm. Clare gave a reading entitled "When may a man be called drunk ?" and Miss A. M. Clare recited " Papa's letter." Mr. George Clarke afterwards gave an instructive address, in the course of which he showed the harmony existing between temperance principles and the teachings of the Old and New Testamente, and maintained that they as Christians should abstain from that which lead others astray. After a song from Mr. Wm Clare, " Which way is your musket a-pintin," a pleasant meeting was brought to ^se with prayer.

.WARRINGTON CIIAMB ;,.R. OF COMMERCE. An important meeting of the Council was held at the Chambers in Bewseye3tree., on Wednesday, when commu- nications were read as to the Mersey Deck and Harbour Board, and a memorial to be forwarded to the Board of Trade was prepared as follovre:—" The memorial of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce respectfully showeth that your memorialists are deeply interested in the trade of Warrington and the surrounding district. including the port of Liverpool, by which their manufactures are priccipally exported. Your memorialists have ascertained that the principal railway companies in the kingdom intend to bring forward during the present session of Parliament bills for increasing the rates which they are now authorised to levy for the carriage of goods, and for legalising and extending their present doubtful rights in respect of terminal charges. Several of your memorialists have established large works in Warrington and its neighbourhood, which will be seriously affected if the railway companies are allowed to , charge the increased rates which are set forth in their bills. At present your memorialists are only liable by law to nay upon certain large quantities of the material they manufac- ture at the rate of lid er 111 per ton per mile, put upon the new scale proposed they would be liable to pay from 111 to 211 per ton per mile. Such en increase of rates would be most injurious to your memorialists. Your memorialiats are further deeply dissatisfied with the manner in which the aforesaid bills deal with the question of terminal charges. Your memorialists believe that a rail- way company is not by law entitled to make terminal charges in reep-ct to any services which form part of the duty and business of a common carrier, and your memorialists humbly pray that this may be declared to be the law, and that any ether services which are not incidental to the business of a carrier, and in respect of which railway companies claim to make charge?, may be dietinctly speci- fied and the charge determined, and that no railway eonpany be allowed to enforce such charges unless an agreement has been made with the parties sought to be charged or until the Railway Commissioners have cdrtified that such charges are reasonable and proper. Your memorialists annex scale of rates which the Landau and North-Western Railway Company can now legally charge in respect of various articles dealt in at Warrington, and al eo the scale which they seek to charge in their new bill. Your memorialists consider that the powers of railway companies, under the most strict supervision, are of an arbitrary character; that it is a great hardship upon traders that these powers are in any way undefined or uncertain, as it is impossible, for pecuniary reasons, that traders should bring their griev- ances before legal tribunals or contest disputed points with powerful corporations. Your memorialists therefore humbly pray that the unsettled questions referred to herein may be put upon a plain and unmistakable footing, and that rail- way companies may not be permitted to make am? addition to the rates which they are at present authorised to charge. Charles Broadbent, president of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce; Joseph Davie?, honorary secretary, January, 1885 —The hon. Secretary was instructed to embody in the report for the annual meeting the following reductions in the local railway rates from Warrington, which had been obtained by the Chamber from the Railway Conference at Norman- ton, viz :—(a) The present rate of 3e 91 per ton for iron Class A Warrington with Liverpool and Birkenhead will be reduced to 3s .1.1 per ton S. to S. 2 ton lots. (1) The rate for Indigo,London with Warrington of 503 per ton will be reduced to 40s. per ton C. and D. (c) Rates, as follow, for Flint glass, 0. R. Warrington with London (nos 34s 2d) will be -32 s 6.1 per ton C. and D. Leicester (now 258 5.1) will be 259 per ton C. and D. Manchester (now is 46) will be 6s 81) per ton S. to S. These reductions are, as far as they go, considered satisfattory.

THE EARLESTOWN SWEEP AND HIS NEIGHBOURS. A great deal of amusement was occasioned at the Newton Petty Sessiens on Saturday, when John Carlin, of Prince's- street, Earlestewti, familiarly known as "The Earlestown Sweep," brought a charge of assault against Edward Mill- ward, one of his neighbours, who carries on a small business as a confectioner. The defendant we represented by Mr. H. L Riley, of St. Helens; and the magistrates on the 143 nett were Messrs. George McCorquodale, R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and C. Pilkington.—On the case being called, the defendant, in reply to the charge, said he would plead guilty with great provocation.—The Chairman: That will hardly do.—Mr. Riley: That is guilty, sir.—The Chair- man : Do you plead guilty ?—Defendant: Yes, sir—The complainant was proceeding with his statement, whereupon Mr. Riley said: I appear for the defendant, and I should like to have the complainant on his oatte—The Chairman: But the defendant pleads guilty.—Mr. Riley: Yes, he pleads guilty, but you will fired out why. As your worships are aware, at Quarter Sessions nothing is more common than when caunsel really believes his client to be guilty to hive the complainant put on oath. I wish to ask the com- plainant questions to show circumstances in extenuation. —The Clerk: Well, had you better not withdraw the plea of guilty, and then go into the case p-operly ?—The Chair- man: He could amend his plea. I don't recollect an in- stance when a complainant was sworn after a plea of guilty.—The Clerk stated that the defendant weuld with- draw his plea of guilty and plead not guilty.—John Carlin, the complainant, was then sworn. His evidence, and the style in which it was given, created considerable laughter. He said that between three and four o'clock on the afternoon of Saturday, the 27th ult., his was " teeming " some boiling water out of a pan full of potatoes in the yard, when the defendant cams out of his own house and asked "What have you been saying about my ' missis ' ? " He (complainant) replied " I have not spoken to your missis 'to-day. It is a long time since I spoke to her" Defendant then struck him five times unawares ; and he exclaimed " Oh, that's your little game, is it 2" The defendant said "Yes," and he (complainant) then said " I won't hit you back ;" and his son added, "Don't hit him back, father, summon him."—Mr. Riley : The defendant keeps a confectioner's shop. doesn't he ? It is more like a lodging-house than a confectioner's shop.—Mr. Riley : And you have expressed your opinion as to the character of the shop and the defendant's wife—told the neighbours that is',e is a very dirty woman and so on Complainant (in surprise) : I have? Da you say so ?—Mr. Riley : I am asking you.—Complainant : No I have not. She telle the neighbours herself by her actions. (Laughter.)—Mr. Riley: Perhaps you draw attention to her actions? Complainant : No, sir, because I don't need to do that. (Renewed laughter.) —la reply to further questions complainant denied having told the defendant's wife that she would go mad like her sister.—Mr. Riley: How long did the affair last? The whole affair lasted about a minute, but it might have las- ted longer if I had gone out to fight like him. (Laughter.) —What did he strike you with? He struck at me SMIle as if he was practising at one of those thumping machines on the market. (Renewed laughter.)—The Clerk (to complain- ant) : Have von any witness ? Complainant : Yes, our Willy. (A laugh.)—He loudly called out in the Court "Willy," amid some laughter, and a lad of abut twelve stepped forward. He simply stated that he saw the defend- ant strike his father five or six times.—Mr. Riley then ad- dressed the Court at some length on behalf of the defendant —The Chairman said the Bench were inclined to take a very lenient view of the matter, but there was no doubt whatever that defendant had broken the law. Tbey hoped he would take a warning by it. He would be let off on the payment of costs. NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIOI MONTHLY MEETING. A monthly meeting of the Newton Improvement Corn. missioners was held at the Town Hall, Newton, on Monday afternoon, when there were psesent :—Messrs. W F Gooch (chairman), J E Pardey, George McCoreuodale, J W Ern- matt, T Stone, B B Glover, T Forster, J H Woesley (law. clerk), and R Brierley (surveyor.) THE LATE EPIDEMIC OF E. CXRLET FEVER.--Aftor the minutes of the last meeting had been read and confirmed Mr. J. W. Emmett remarked that he was pleased to notice that the fever in that neighbourhood, particularly in E ales- town, was decreasing and had decreased considerably since their last meeting. He understood their medical officer to say that there had only been four cases reported since 25th of December. Whether that was from the frost or the extra precautions that the public had taken he did not say, but he '(Mr. Emmett) had no doubt it was due to both the public having been more careful in not running into one another's houses and the severe frost they had had. It was very pleasing to him (Mr: Emmett), and he hoped it would !ee to the public. TEE NEW CEMETERY.—At a meeting of the Highways, Public Works, and Sanitary Committee, held on the 15th December, the committee resolved upon the allotment of certain portions of the cemetery land for the use of the Church of England, Nonconformists, and Roman Catholics, and also that the same fees now paid to' the minister and sexton at Wargrave Church be adopted for the Church of England portion of the cemetery. The Surveyor certified the sum of £lOO, due to Mr. J. Penniagton on his sewer and road contract at Wargrave, and the sum of £2OO, due to Mr. J. Rothwell on his building contract at the cemetery. Cheques for these amounts were ordered to be signed. The committee held a special meeting on the sth inst, at which a proof of the proposed regulations and scale of fees for

RUNCORN. GALLANT CONDUCT OF A RUNCORN CAPTAIN. 11,1TRUESTING PRESENTATIag. The Custom Rouse, Runcorn, was the scene of a very in- teresting ceremony on Monday, when Captain Thos. Paul, master of the schooner Gleaner, of Runcorn, was preeented with a commemorative silver medal. There were present Mr. F. Samone (collector of customs), the Rey. W. and Mrs. Vase ; Mrs. Lloyd, Mrs. Walton, Captains Le Coutier, P. Sinnot, Hulse, Atherton, Sherlock,; and Messrs W. Shaw (seamen's missionary), George Moss ,J. Burrows, R. Beckett, J. Harty, IL Berry, I. Garner, J. Pritchard (manazing owner of the Gleaner), and a number of seamen. Mr. Simons said he had been requested by the Board of Trade to take upon himself the honour of presenting to Captain Paul, on behalf of the Italian Government, a Cam- memorative medal adjudged by the Min'ster of Marine as a mark Of gratitude for having rescued, on the 16th February last, and landed at Sligo, the crew of ten men of the Italian brigantine Luigi, Thiel] was wrecked on a voyage from Car- diff to Buenos Apes. He trusted that their British sailors would never be found wanting in humanity on the high seas. Their pluck and bravery were well known all the world over, and he hoped they would long maintain that charac- ter. There were SOllle people of opinion that their sailors were deteriorating in seamanship. However that might be, he for his part did not believe in it, an?, he was quite sure that whenever their services were required they would ever display that true gallantry which had always distinguished them. He wished Captain Paul long life, and ho hoped he would hand down the medal now presented as an heirloom to his posterity, and that it might be a memento of the heroic deed which had been performed by him in the hour of peril. He trusted that he would never have to rescue anether crew under similar circumstences, but should he ever be called upon in the future he was sure that neither he nor his crew would be found wanting. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Pritchard read the following report from Captain Paul, dated Sligo, 20th February, 1884 :—" Dear Sir,—As wired you yesterday, I arrived safely here after a wild pas- sage. We sailed from Margate-roads on the 14th inst., and after sailing from the Longships 67 miles sighted a vessel apparently in distress. We hove down upon her and found her to be the Italian brig Luigi of Genoa, and fast sinking, after being in collision with some three-master brigantine unknown aboat two o'clock on the morning of the 16. h inst. We remained by her about three hours, and after some difficulty and trouble managed to take the crew on board the schooner. The crew (ten men) were all in a very ex- hausted condition. Wind Lilo ving moderate gale SE. at the time; heavy sea. We then proceeded on our voyage and arrived last night at Sligo. Italian consul for this die- trict is not at home to-day, and I expect he will be here to- morrow and take charge of the shipwrecked crew. We managed to get the boat in and out without damage." Mr. Pritchard added that the total length of time the Italian sailors were on board the Gleaner was about five days. The inscription on the medal which recorded the gallant rescue of the crew was translated by Cap:ain Le Couteur. Captain Paul said it gave him great pleasure to receive the reward, but in rendering the services he considered that he and his crew only did their duty as British seamen. (Hear, hear.) He could assure them that he shoeld never forget parting with the crew after their stay on beard his vessel. The men gave them to understand that their act would never be forgotten, and that their services would be made known to their wives and families. At that moment he felt the parting to be most touching. He returned his thanks to the Italian Government for the medal, while he wished to express his gratitude to Mr. Samons for the in- terest he had taken in that meeting. He hoped and trusted as a British subject he should always be wiling to render assistance te his fellow creatures in the time of need. He returned thanks to those who had attended thet day, while be must not omit to mention the bravery of his crew, and to thank them for the manner in which they conducted themselves, and helped him in his undertaking. Vice-presidente Of Wycliffe Mutual Improvement Society, read an essay before the members on Monday evening, on t. Politics in the Pulpit." The essayist took the negative view of the question, and in an able manner set forth his arguments in support of his viewF. He contended that politics being debatable were entirely out of place in the pulpit, that it was now-a-days unnecessary for ministers of the Gospel to touch upon political subjects. and it was highly inexpedient to preach political sermons, which were frequently disastrous to the welfare of the congregation. The pulpit and the pulpit's opportunities should be used for higher and nobler work; but while he had an objection to political sermons he had not the slightest objection to "political parsons," who had ample opportunity for expres- sing their opinions on the platform, in the newspaper, and in the magazine. He further objected to political sermons, because they encouraged the growing habit of preaching on simply secular subjects, a habit which was greatly to be de- plored. In the discussion which followed. Mr. Coutts found but a single supporter, Mr. George Brown, and his argu- ments were ably refuted by Messrs S. Kenyon, G. Walling. son, T. C. London, and A. Ratbbone, and the Rev. John Tongs. The latter gentlemen presided over the meeting.
