ANNUAL SUPPER.—On Monday about 50 of the employes of the London and North-Western Railway Company from the Bank Quay and Arpley Stations held their annual sup- per at the Patten Arms Hotel, when an excellent repast was provided by the manageress, Miss Shuttleworth. After sup- per Mr. Ashurst was voted to the chair, and Mr. Horobin to the vice-chain—The toast of the Queen and Royal family having been drunk, the London and North-Western Railway followed, and was responded to by Mr. Cotton. The health and welfare of the donors was very enthusiastically drunk. Afterwards a very interesting presentation took place, in the form of a silver medal to Mr. Thomas Warburton on the completion of his 33rd year in the service of the company, and for his invaluable assistance rendered from time to time to widows and orphans of his late fellow-servants.— The Chairman, in making the presentation, spoke very highly of Mr. Warburton's good qualities, remarks which were fully endorsed by several others present —Mr. Warbur- ton, in a very nice speech, thanked his fellow-workmen for I the kindness they bad shown him by adorning his breast with the medal. The medal bore a suitable inscription on one side and a view`of a railway carriage on the other, and W 55 supplied by Messrs E. Eustance and Son, to whom great credit is due for the high finish of the article. During the evening several songs and recitations were very ably rendered by Messrs Richardson, Starkey, Hale, Torkriegton, Whitworth, Limb, Jackson, Whittaker, am A vote of thanks, proposed by Mr Marshall, seconded by Mr. Brook, to the chairman and vice-chairman, brought a very enjoyable evening to a close. SLAUGHTER OF RATS.—On Tuesday afternreen no less than 47 rats were slaughtered in the course of a "hunt." The scene of the "slaughter of the innocents "was a small shed connected with and situate behind the stores of the Earlestown Industrial Co-operative Society in Earle-street ; and the executioners included bakers, shopmen, a brick- setter, a tinker, and other volunteers, whose weapons con- sisted of hayforks and pikele, iron crowbars and iron rode, an iron hammer, and thick pieces of wood. It seems that in one corner of the shed alluded to was a heap of manure, and in the opposite corner Was a large box or chest in whicb provender for the co-operative horses was kept. Early in the afternoon of Tuesday one or two rats were noticed prowling about the place. A bricksetter and one of the employes of the society pat their shoulders to the provender chest, and on raising it they were naturally surprised when a smell army of rats, at least 50 or GO in number, rushed Gut and darted about the premises in all directions. The vermin scampered about the shed, buried themselves in :be nurture, hid amongst the coals, and took refuge under itubs and boxes lying about. About eight or ten persons soon enrolled themselves as " volunteers" in the expedition. An attack on the "enemy" who strategically kept in am- bush, was ordered. The provender chest was next remcved and many rats again came out, but ',was only to their doom. The manure and coal were then removed and as the vermin, which had taken refuge therein, made their appearance they were pounced upon. The "battle" lasted about two hours, and after the conflict exactly 47 dead bodies were counted and placed together in a large box. Several of the rats escaped, seine of them with serious injuries.

Mr. Chlmberlain was unable to attend the proceedings in connection with the Liberal demonstration at Ipswich on Thursday. The right hon. gentleman remained indoors during the day in accordance with the directions of his medical adviser.

ANNEAL BAZAAR AND CHRISTMAS TREE AT CADISREAD. —The annual bazaar and Christmas tree was held on behalf of the trust fund of the Wesleyan Chapel in the d ty school, Cadishead, on New Year's Day. Great credit is due to the day school teacher, Mr. Gatentry, and those associated with him for the arrangement of the stlle and the dressing of the room. One hundred and ninety-three sat down to a most excellent tea, catered for by Mr. and Mrs. Oswald. After tea there was a brisk sale at the various stalls, pre- sided over by Mesdames Johnson, Tort, Jackson, Whitfield, Owen, and Cartwright. The Ipfreshment stall WAS con- ducted by Miss Johnston and Miss Toft. The performing dog, kindly introduced by a friend, drew a good number of the young people. The curiosity room was an additional' attraction. The Christmas tree in the centre of the room. its spreading branches decorated with different toys was a great attraction to the children. Upon the whole the bazaar passed off with satisfaction, the net proceeds being £37 103 10d. - -

--• Panne Eowano's MAJOUITY.—The festivities in con- nection with the coming of age of Prince Albert Victor concluded on Saturday, when the Royal party had a spin with the West Norfolk hounds. Count Milaster, German Ambassador, arrived at Sandringham on Saturday, and on behalf of the Emperor of Germany presented his Royal Highness with the Order of the Black Eagle. A Corres- pondent writes—" Apropos of Prince Edward's proper name. His father always calls him Edward, and his name in the family is Eddy ; but he himself signs in full Albeit Victor.' I have seen both telegrams and letters from him within the last few days, and in every case Albert Victor is his style. So people may call him Edward, as the Prince of Wales would like ; or Albert Victor, as the Queen desires, and the young Prince himself does in all formal writing." Prince Edward is certainly the mon convenient title, and if, as is said, this is to be the name used in the event of accession to the Throne, why not adopt it at once The following is a copy of a letter which Prince Edward re- ceived from Mr. Gladstone on the attainment of his Royal Highness' majority Hawarden Castle, January 7th. Sir,—As the oldest among the confidential servants of her Majesty, I cannot allow the anniversary to pass without notice which will to-morrow bring your Royal Highness to full age, and thus mark an important epoch in your life. The hopes and intentions of those whose lives lie, like mine, in the past, are of little moment; but they have seen much, and what they have seen suggests much for ae future. There lies before your Royal Highness in prospect the oc- cupation—l trust at a distant date—of a Throne which, to me at least, appears the most illustrious in the world from ite history and associations, from its legal basis, from the weight of the cares it brings, from the loyal love of the people, and from the unparelled opportunities it gives, in so many ways and in so many regions, of doing good to the al- most countless numbers whom the Almighty has placed be- neath the sceptre of Eogland. I fervently (desire and pray and their cannot be a more animating prayer—that your Royal Highness may ever grow in the principles of con- duct, and may be adorned with all the qu dities which cor- respond with this great and noble vscation. And, sir, if sovereignty has been relieved by our modern institutions of some of its burdens, it will, I believe, remain true that there has been no period of the world's history at which successors to the monarchy could more efficaciously con- tribute to the stability of a great historic system, dependent even more upon love than upon strength, by devotion to their duties,and by a bright example to the country. This result we have happily been permitted to see, and other generations will, I trust, witness it anew. Heartily desiring that in the life of your Royal Highness every private and personal may be joined with every public blessing, I have the honour to remain, sir. your Royal Highness's most duti- ful and faithful servant, W. E. GrunsToNE.—To H.R.H. Prince Albert Victor." Mr. Gladstone has rec, iced a letter from Prince Albert Victor, in reply to the birthday can- gratulations of the right hon. gentleman. His Royal High- ness, when assuring the Prime Minister that the letter shall have that attention which words from him must deserve, describes it as admirably indicating much which demands his most earnest thought, and expresses his gratitude for the Premier's remembrances.

SINGULAR AFFILIATION CASE—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and C. Pilkington, an affiliation case of an un- usual character was heard. The defendant was Jonathan lienwright,a well-known extensive farmer at Buttonwood, and on his behalf Mr. Percy Davies, of Warrington, ap- , peare,i ; while the complainant was Mary Ann Dutton, who seas formerly in his employ as a housekeeper, and was repre- sented by Mr. Arthur Browne, of Warrington.--Mr. Browne stated that the complaisant at present resided at Crown- street, Earlestown, and was a single woman. For over two years she had lived as housekeeper at the defendant's house, the defendant being a large farmer at Buttonwood. Inti- macy appeared to have existed between the parties for a con- siderable time, but he (Mr. Browne) could nrodues no really cerroborative evidence. The ekfentlant had, however, been ac- cused of being the father of the complainant's child, and he then said that he was not compelled to stay in this country and be could run away. He would rely upon that fact as corroborative testimony. In addition the defendant had offered the complainant £5 to take a certain decoction he 1, had prepared, but the complainant refused to do this ; and ' since the birth of the child he had verbally offered to pay her Be per week. Unfortunately, however, there was no witness preient except the complainant when that offer was made.—The complainant, May Ann Dutton, was then celled, and gave evidence in support of Mr. Browne's state- ment. She was closely cross-examined at great length by Mr. Davies. She denied having gone " sweethe acting" with anybody.—Several witnesses were called, the defence being a denial of the alleged paternity.—The Bench ulti- mately made an order for the defendant to pee, the sum of 45 per week with the usual costs.—Mr. Davies gave notice of appeal.

div.head: TRUTHFULNESS OF G_EORGE WASHINGTON.
div.p: THE TRUTHFULNESS OF G_EORGE WASHINGTON.

All have beard the anecdote of Gladstone and his axe, but few of the story how, on one occasion, Ge irge Washington met a dearly loved friend totting 'along the street on crutches —one foot in a sling and swathed in bandages —witn excrucia- ting agony depleted on his countenance. "What," said the compassionate General, is the reason Of this?' Dolefully came the reply, "Gout." The great man paused, and, with his usual veracity, said, there is but ONE remedy for this great scourge. Take my advic,., and go to the nea-est chemist and get a bottle of REYNOLDS' GOUT bl'Et. I BIC. I speak from experiesce when I assure you that this remarkably and most efficacious medicine is the ONLY safe and truly reli- able core." The adv:ce was readily accepted, and never again has this sufferer experienced the terrible pain he was then en- during.

div.head: TiE BIRMINGHAM UNEMPLOYED.— On Friday another
div.p: TiE BIRMINGHAM UNEMPLOYED.— On Friday another

- great demonstration of the unemployed took place in Bir- I mingham. several thousand perssns marching through the principal streets .shouting •• We want work," and "This will show them whether there is any distress." The man, Thomas Woodward, who was arrested on Thursday for steal- ing a loaf while in the procession of the unemployed, was discharged, the prosecutor declining to give evidence. SHOCKING ACCIDENTS AT SOLLINGTON.—TWO shocking accidents happened at Bollington near Macclesfield, on Fri- day morning. The first was to Alfred Timperley, plumber, who fell down a deep well and was dreadfully injured, and is not expected to recover. Be was to have been married on Sunday. The other was to an o'd man named Turner, who was caught in a shaft at th ! hat works and frightfully in- jured. Both were at once removed to the Macclesfield In- firmary. EXECUTION AT GALWAY.— Michael Downey was execu- ted at Galway gaol at ten minutes after eight o'clock on Friday morning for the murder of John Moylan, at Clonboo. He had made a statement admitting his guilt. Daring the night be slept badly, and took no breakfast in the morning, though he accepted a glass of wine. He bore himself with great calmness at the scaffold, and death appeared to be instantaneous. Berry was the executioner, assisted by a man named Chester. THE ALLEGED CONSPIRACY TO MURDER A Carr.m.--The trial of William J.mes, Thomas Long, and George Fletcher Walker, on a charge of conspiracy to murder an infant, was resumed at the Old Bailey, London. on Friday. Mr. Bosley addressed the jury ox behalf of Walker. The jury found Long guilty, and Jones and Walker not guilty.—The learned judge in passing sentence, said he was of opinion that the jury bad found a very proper and discriminating verdict, and that neither Jones nor Walker had ever contem- plated destroying the life of the child. With regard to Long the case was vary different, and he accordingly sentenced him to eight years' penal servitude. THEA "WORLD" LIBEL CASE: MR. YATES IMPRI- SONED.—In the Court of Appeal, on Friday, judgment was delivered in the Case of Yates v. The Queen. The appeal for erred of judgment from the Queen's Bench was argued on Tuesday and Wednesday, arising out of a libel on Lord Lonsdale. The Master of the Rolls said the Court had no , jurisdiction with regard to the case, except as upon a writ lof error. He held that the application for information was prior to the commencement of the prosecution, and there- fore the fiat of the Attorney-General was unnecessary for such application.—Lord Justice Cotton concurrred.—The judgment of the Court below was confirmed.—At the close of the proceedings. Mr. Yates, editor of the World, who during the afternoon had occupied a seat next to bee soli- tor in the well of the court, surrendered to the tipstaff, and after shaking hands with Mr. Edward Clarke, QC., and other gentlemen in court, was removed in custody during his incarceration, which is for a period of four months. Mr. Yates will be treated as a first-class misde- I meanant. It is stated that Mr. Yates will not appeal to the House of Lords against the decision of the Court of Ap- peal.

div.head: SUPPOSED LOSS OF A CHANNEL STEAMER.
div.p: SUPPOSED LOSS OF A CHANNEL STEAMER.

The Holyhead correspondent of the Central News tele- graphing last evening says :—Much anxiety is felt here re- specting the safety of the paddle steamer Admiral Moorson, belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany's fleet. She left Dublin at noon on Thursday with a cargo and a few passengers, and was due at Holyhead at half-past six last evening. She has not yet arrived, and the opinion is fast gals lug ground that she must have been lost. Every steamer arriving here is most eagerly watched from shore by crowds ef expectant persons, among whom are very prominent the wifes and children of the missing crew. At four p.m. on Thursday, she was met coming from Dublin by the mail steamer Munster, and about mid-channe by the express steamer Shamrock, and should in ordinary course have, half an hour afterwards, been passed by the North Wall boat from Holyhead to Dublin, but the crew of that steamer did net see her. She has not been seen since by any vessel from this port, and the town is in the greatest excitement. She had a cargo of over eight hundred tons, about six hundred and sixty live pigs, thirty-four cattle, and six passengers, two of whom were cattle dealers, two aoldiers, and two females. A late telegram says :—lt is stated that the collision at Stoke to-day was caused by the driver of the former run- ning past the signals, which were against him. The driver died this evening from the terrible injuries he received, but the stoker, although badly Injured, is not in any danger.

div.head: ALARMING RAILWAY ACCIDENT.
div.p: ALARMING RAILWAY ACCIDENT.

An alarming railway accident has occurred near Stoke- upon-Trent on Friday morning, attended, it is reported, with serious results. The through 5-15 express from Man- chester to Birmingham, due at Stoke at 10-20, had left Stoke station, and was passing the siding near the Dike of Sutherland's, and about two miles on the Stafford side of the station, at full speed when it ran into a mineral train which was straight across the line. The collision was terrible, the passenger engine and most of the carriages being thrown off and scattered about the line in great confusion. The driver and stoker of the passenger train have been re- moved to the North Stafford Infirmary with severe injuries. Medical men,. have been despatched from Stoke to the scene of the catastrophe, and a breakdown gang has been sent to assist in clearing the line, which is completely blocked, and traffic therefore at a standstill. A later telegram states :—The passengers were brought on to Stoke as soon as possible, and after some delay all were able to resume their journey not much the worse for the accident. Fortunately, the two first compartments of the passenger train were kept empty. The engine and three compartments were wrecked. The train was heavily freighted, and there were many miraculous escapes. None of the officials can account for the mineral train being across the line at the time the express train was due. A Central News correspondent telegraphs :—The driver of the express mistook his own signal, which was against him, for one in- tended for the driver of a goods train backing into a siding. The engines came in contact, the express being thrown off the metals on to its aide. Both the driver and stoker are seriously hurt, bet the passengers escaped injury. There were very few people in the train.

div.head: FIANCE AND CHINA.
div.p: FIANCE AND CHINA.
PARTS, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—GeneraI Da Lisle tele- graphs that he has completed preparations for advance to the Chinese frontiers. THE RETURN ROUTE FROM KHARTOUM.

- _ The Daily News understands that if Lord Wolseley should decide to make use of tbe Suakim road for the return of some of the refugees from the Soudan, a small addi- tional force will be despatched thither in order to aid the withdrawal. DESPATCH PttOM LORD_ WOLESLEY.

Lord Wolesley telegraphil from Korti on Friday after- noon :—Kitchener returned from Gakdul to-day. He left It early on the fourteenth. Stewart was to start same after- noon for Metammeh, leaving Colonel Vandelent, of the Sussex Regiment, to command there. The guards, during their occupation; did good werk ; built two forts; arranged Zarebas and made roads. The people in the neighbour- hood have not come in yet. They call us Turks, and can- not discriminate between them and B:shi Bazoulss, and are not convinced that their treatment will be good. Gakdul is healthy •, all quiet in the neighbourhood. There are twelve wells at Howeitfat ; five in working order, and the remainder gradually repairing. The water is good.

_ ELECTION OF A GUARDIAN FOR NEWTON.— Notices have been issued stating that the vacancy in the representa- tion of Newton on the Warrington Board of Guardians will b) shortly filled up. The Local Government Board have given their sanction to tbe election of a Guardian, and nominations of suitable candidates must be made and delivered after the 16th, but on or before the 21st January, to Mr James C Sutton, clerk to the Guardians, or to Mr Joseph Caldwell, Newton, who are the only persons author- ised to receive the same. On the 22nd a list of the nomina- -1 tions will be suspended in the Board-room and at the princi- pal external gate of the Workhouse. In case more than one candidate is nominated, the voting papers will be delivered on the 29th inst., collected on the 30th, and on the following day Mr Sutton, as returning officer, will proceed to count the number of votes. ___ .

ALLEGED THEFT OF A WATCH.—At the Borough Court on Thursday, Robert Haines (28), glass and china rivetter, of no settled abode, was charged with stealing in December last, from the hence of James Rimmer, fitter, 21, Gladstone- street, a silver lever watch, of the value of £4. On the evening of the 12Lh December the house of Mr. Rimmer was forcibly entered and the watch stolen, in addition to other articles. Information was given to the police, and en the Bth inst Chief Constable Hunt received a communi- cation from the Manchester police stating that there was a man in custody at Manchester, who had been endeavouring to dispose of a watch case that answered to the description of the missing one, was the same number, and had on it an inscription setting forth that it was presented to James Rim- mer in 1859. Prisoner, who denied the theft, was also charged with receiving the watch knowing it to have been stolen. To this charge he pleaded guilty, and was sent to prison for three months with hard labour.
